Senator ANANDA-RAJAH (Victoria) (10:48): I wish to make some comments regarding the process that has followed the Greens political party and the coalition thwarting passage of an improvement to our generational aged-care reforms. As you know, this government is committed to improving standards, quality, accessibility and affordability of aged care, and we had to do it, because when we came to office in 2022 we inherited an aged-care system that was in crisis. It was the royal commission that demanded we draw a line under a coalition era that they titled as 'neglect'. With that, we began the hard work of generational reform.

It was in November of last year that the new Aged Care Act kicked off. This was a complete overhaul of the system. It was recommendation 28 of the royal commission that demanded we introduce a more streamlined assessment system for older Australians. Until then, there had been way too much duplication, inefficiency and undue complexity. In other words, it was onerous and burdensome on Australians, and, frankly, it was expensive for taxpayers. That's what happens when you have inefficiencies and duplication. And so, over a number of years, starting in 2020, the department started to craft an assessment tool that is now called the IAT, the integrated assessment tool, which has received a lot of press, not all positive, and there has also been a lot of mischaracterisation of this tool and the rationale behind having it.

We introduced this tool because we realised that there was imperfect decision-making happening by humans. Some people were getting too much in their home packages; others were not getting enough. If you were a man and you spoke perfect English, the chances are you were going to get a pretty good package, maybe overcompensated for your needs. If, on the other hand, you were a non-English-speaking migrant—a bit like my family, my dad—the chances are you were probably going to miss out and not have your needs met. In fact, that's what the data showed. We had $4 billion in unallocated funds that were sitting in accounts not being used. So something had to be done to deliver consistency and standardisation.

The IAT was developed over a number of years using very large datasets, using expert input. I won't go through all of that. It is in the Hansard from 1 April 2026, which lays out very clearly how this was developed. It basically then used about 13 different sections, including social supports, health issues and the home environment, to classify an older Australian into one of eight categories, No. 8 being the most severe category. With that, we also applied a prioritisation mechanism. We know the process is not perfect, and that was recognised by this minister very early on. And so we instigated what was called a rapid review into the prioritisation mechanism.

I'm going through this because the detail matters. It was a prioritisation mechanism that underwent a rapid review. The report is currently being considered by the government, but changes were made, and you have to be agile when you're introducing generational reform. Things never go smoothly. There are always roadblocks. There are always points of friction. We have tried to be adaptive as a government. And so it became clear very early on that patients with, for example, motor neurone disease needed to be escalated up in the categories. So they now have a categorisation of 'urgent', which means they get their care packages, their Support at Home care packages, within a month, as do other people in that urgent category. But we know that the prioritisation mechanism does need to be adjusted, and that is being considered right now.

What is disappointing, after weeks and weeks and weeks of testimony and hearings that I've sat through in the committee with my colleagues from the Greens political party and the coalition, is that, now, five minutes to midnight, as we are trying to fix this system and make it more responsive to the needs of older Australians, they basically have banded together to completely thwart this. They are throwing the baby out with the bathwater. The point of contention is the escalation pathway. They are blocking passage of an escalation pathway that we want to introduce so that older Australians get the care that they need, the packages that they need, in a much faster, more streamlined fashion. Why? They want us to go back to the drawing board and tear up the IAT, the integrated assessment tool, because they say that it is an algorithm. God forbid we use an algorithm to deliver efficiency, consistency and standardisation! Humans are the best decision-makers! That is absolutely false. In medicine, humans are not the best decision-makers. Humans are assisted by similar clinical decision tools. We have a plethora of them in health care because we recognise that humans are biased decision-makers. And so, when we're dealing with thousands upon thousands of older Australians who need aged care, we must deliver consistency across what is a very diverse population terms of income status, ethnicity, language and values, as well. But we have to deliver equity and standardisation. And so it is beyond disappointing that this has been blocked by the coalition and the Greens political party.

In addition, I want to also mention that this goes contrary to several peak groups who provided testimony. Mr Craig Gear of OPAN described this escalation pathway as, I quote, 'an important interim reform' and argued:
Older people need an accessible correction mechanism while longer-term reform goes on.

And that's what they're blocking. They're not happy. They want to throw the baby out with the bathwater. 'Get rid of the IAT,' they say, but in doing so they are stopping us from actually improving the system, stopping government the from being agile and responsive to the needs of older Australians. They're going contrary to these peak bodies, who are actually saying: 'Get on with it. We know that it's not perfect, but get on with it.' Then we have Mr Irlam of COTA Australia, who said that further work on the assessment process, quote, 'should not delay fixing the immediate problem affecting older people'. Ageing Australia similarly supported the escalation pathway proceeding while broader work on the process continued. Mr Symondson from Ageing Australia said:

If we go right back to the drawing board now, how many people are going to fall through the already gaping cracks that we have in the system while we get that right? Which is why we do support the amendment …

We have a range of stakeholders—peak groups—urging this parliament to get on with it and deliver on this significant reform, which is an escalation pathway, which does put in the human so that we have a practical safeguard that is designed to improve the prioritisation mechanism for Australians who feel like they haven't been heard or haven't been properly assessed by the IAT. We think that number, based on data from earlier this year during estimates, is about 0.5 per cent. But, over a large number of people, that's a lot of people. We recognise that it's not perfect, and we are trying to fix it by introducing an escalation pathway with a qualified assessor. They're making that judgement, responding to the issues raised by older Australians and their families.

But the Greens, in their wisdom, and the coalition have said, 'No can do.' Start again, government. To all those years of work in trying to come up with a more efficient, standardised, better process in response to recommendation 28 of the royal commission, they say: 'It's not good enough for us. We want to go back to the old system—' because the old system was perfect. What nonsense. It was not perfect; $4 billion tells us of unallocated funds—unallocated meaning not being used—because the assessments were wrong. It tells us that the old system was not perfect. We are trying to improve this system, and you are standing in the way as usual. The Greens political party put the perfect in front of the good. They are not pragmatists. They do not have the interests of older Australians in mind.

This reform also introduces the Aboriginal aged care commissioner. This is not a point of contention, but it is urgent that we deliver on this reform, because older Australians, particularly those of Indigenous background, have woeful health outcomes. ABS data from 2022 put the life expectancy gap at nine years for men and eight years for women. However, if you live in a remote or very remote community, life expectancy is 67 years for men and 71 for women. It is much, much worse.

We know that older Indigenous Australians have a much harder time gaining access to aged care, for a range of reasons. Of course, the tyranny of distance is one of them, but they find the system hostile. They lack trust in the system. This is the legacy of colonisation. So recommendation 49 from the royal commission said that we should consider appointing an Aboriginal aged-care commissioner in order to be responsive to the cultural needs of Indigenous Australians right around this country, because they don't feel like they have cultural safety in the current system. They need an advocate. They lack the self-efficacy and the ability to advocate for themselves. So an interim commissioner was installed by us in 2024, and we now want this enshrined in legislation going forward.
Senator Ruston: Very good idea. We support that.
Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: I'm glad you support it, Senator Ruston. I do accept that.
Senator Allman-Payne interjecting—

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH: And so do you, Senator Allman-Payne. However, I am disappointed that we are being thwarted in delivering what are much-needed and urgent improvements to the assessment system. We know that generational reform is never easy. We're going through it right now with the NDIS. That's going to be a bumpy road. No-one's pretending that delivering generational reform in aged care is going to be simple. We all accept that there are going to be bumps on the road. But what we don't need, as a government and on behalf of the Australian people, are parliamentarians turning the needs of older Australians into a political football. We've got to rise above this, folks. There's too much at stake. There are people out there suffering.

I have some lived experience with that, with my 86-year-old father, who didn't actually wait that long to get his IAT done—but it was on us. We as a family probably did not make that decision to actually seek help early enough. So to older Australians out there: I urge you to not leave it too late. If you think you need an assessment, get the assessment done, while we bat it out in here and try to deliver on this escalation pathway so that we can, in those instances where you feel like you have not received a satisfactory assessment, escalate it, get it amended and ensure that you are heard through a proper process. Instead, we sit here wasting time instead of serving the nation, playing politics with the needs of older Australians. It's disgraceful. The Greens political party should hang its head in shame. There is no point crying tears on committees. Get in here and actually act. (Time expired)

Senator STEWART: As a Mutthi Mutthi Wamba Wamba woman, this bill speaks to something that's really important for our community, and it goes to the importance of elders, and the respect for elders and the place that we hold elders in, in our community. For so many of our community members, the burden of taking care of our elders has been mostly borne by our families, like so many families. That is for a number of reasons, and certainly a big one is that the institutions and the mainstream services that are out there, that are supposed to take care of our elders, are not seen as safe places for our community members. That is because of past practices and policies in this country, where our elders have been institutionalised. So the idea of going into another institution in your older years can actually be really triggering for our elders.

So having a role such as the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner is really important. It will be a position, a person, an opportunity, for our elders, when they are having challenges with the systems or the services—somewhere where they can raise their voices and be confident that the person on the other end understands their circumstances and has the understanding of their lived experience of being an Aboriginal person in this country that really only comes from having a shared experience of growing up black in this country. I think it's really important that we get the opportunity to have this conversation in the Senate and put the case for why it's important and why we should not play politics with something like this in this place.

Our elders are our teachers, our storytellers and our knowledge holders. They are the people who hold all of the information about the generations that came before us. It is one of the many reasons they are so esteemed in our community. They carry language. They carry culture. They carry our family history. I've certainly got people in my family who are like walking family trees. I'm not one of those people! But certainly our elders carry the responsibility of holding that knowledge for us and of handing it down.

Aged-care services aren't just about services. They are about giving Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander elders the dignity, the care and the respect that they deserve. There are so many services that our community access that don't treat them in the way that the rest of Australians get treated, and aged care is another one of those places where you can see the impact that that has on our elders. I know that dignity and respect look different depending on who you are, and that is right. If you are from a different multicultural background or from the broader Australian community, your idea of what good care looks like—at what dignified care looks like—is going to be different to what the care for an Aboriginal elder might look like. For us, it means being close to your family. It means staying connected to country and being around people who understand you and how you've grown up and that shared experience.

It's important that you get cared for by people who understand you. Especially as you get older, you might end up with something like dementia. It means there may be a whole bunch of things in your environment that trigger you, that bring back some trauma and some memories and make a place feel really unsafe for you. The stakes are even higher for elders when they go into services, and they should have the opportunity to feel safe and loved and understood and cared for. As they age and become more vulnerable, it's really important that we look after them in a way that they deserve. That's for a multitude of reasons. Our elders are people who have contributed to their families and to the community. They've contributed to our national economy over their lifetime too. They've been taxpayers. They deserve to have dignity in care as they get older. This bill really does take an important step towards delivering that for our elders. It's an important step that we're taking in the parliament today.

The other part of this is that it was an important recommendation of the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety. The case for it is really clear. We know that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are more likely to need this type of care earlier. I could rattle off all the statistics on all the ways that we are struggling in health outcomes and determinants. All those things mean that we're more likely to need the services that aged care has the ability to deliver earlier in our lives. So it is important that we do this.

When people aren't engaging in aged-care services, it's not necessarily because they don't need to. It's because they don't feel like it's safe. That means that the delaying of care, treatment or the services they need actually makes their health worse. It costs the system more. Not that it's all about dollars—this is about actually caring about the human at the other end of the service—but the putting off or the delaying of care because you're worried about how you might be treated or about someone's ability to understand you and your needs should be concerning for all of us. Too many elders have been asked to leave their communities to receive that care and to be separate from their families, isolated from culture and receive services from people who don't speak their language.

I think it is really important that we have a position like this aged-care commission position, one that can hear the concerns that people have and advocate for them in the kinds of places that can be really intimidating—places like this or broader forums of aged-care services. There's also, of course, all the intricacies of all the different bits and pieces of legislation, regulations, policies or funding that people might not know about. It's important that there is a role that people feel they can go to, to have their voices heard in a way that's safe and that sees them.

A position like this is an important marker, too; it acknowledges the history of our country in terms of some of the reasons people might not feel safe in the aged-care system. This position takes a step in acknowledging that really harmful history we've had in this country by saying that we need an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and that the services and the engagement that we might need to undertake or deliver for Aboriginal elders might look a bit different. The advocacy might look a bit different, and that requires a role, in the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commissioner, so that we can deliver for our communities. It recognises that cultural safety isn't just a box-ticking exercise; it's something that we need to be able to do and deliver. It's really fundamental to delivering good care. It's not just—

What we have found in this parliament, under the current Labor government, is that the Prime Minister determines the staffing numbers for whichever political party or Independent, right across this whole chamber. I think it's terribly wrong, what is happening here. The Prime Minister's office should not determine who gets staffing and how many staff they have.

The number of personal advisers that One Nation has is five. That's for six members of parliament. The Labor Party has 507. The Prime Minister personally has 59 staff. If you look at the Liberal Party, Angus Taylor has 35 personal staff. If you look at Senator Payman—I'll speak on her behalf as well—she's got none. Why? It's because she dared to walk away from the Labor Party. So those people who do not support the Labor Party are getting punished through not having the staffing.

What we have requested is an inquiry into this. Who's going to block it? The Liberal Party. The Liberal and National parties want to block this. Why? Are we all treated fairly, across the range of political parties? No. Basically, it is: 'Let's hurt the ones who do not support us. Let's hurt the ones who are not led like sheep in this place and who have a voice for the Australian people. Let's hurt them by denying them the staff that they need to run their offices.' It is quite clear.

What I find amazing is that, although the government has also damaged the coalition—a loss to their staff—the coalition says, 'We don't want to have an inquiry into this.' They're shutting down the inquiry. So it's the uniparty again. I want the public to know this. It is the uniparty again colluding to cause as much damage as they can to the independent ones who were elected to the parliament. And I think it's wrong.

There have been some comments, including from, just off the top of my head, Senator McGrath. He said in a comment that it is 'vindictive'. Senator McGrath said that, but he's not standing up to support an inquiry. Isn't it funny! You just say these things to suit you at the time, but, when push comes to shove as far as putting it to an inquiry, you don't want to. Why doesn't the Liberal Party want to put it before an inquiry?

As far as I'm concerned, the Prime Minister should have no right to determine what staff levels are given out to crossbenchers or members of any party, whether they're in the lower house or the upper house. If we have a separate board that determines the wages, then why don't we have a separate board that determines the staffing levels—right across the board—for future parliaments? That's where it's important.

This is collusion by the major political parties now to do as much damage as they can to One Nation. Do you know why? You're scared of the rise of One Nation. You think you've had this tied up your way for all this time, and you are now getting challenged—but not by One Nation. You're being challenged by the people of this nation who are fed up with what you've been dishing out to them. They want change. They see that change with One Nation. That's why we won seven seats in South Australia and why we won the seat of Farrer, previously held by the Liberals for 77 years. That's why we won Secret Harbour, held by the Labor Party since 1989. That's why we look like we're going to pick up some seats in Victoria, and Labor will be gone. New South Wales—the same. And this is just a dirty trick again by the major political parties because of One Nation's rise.

All I'm asking for is what is fair. All I'm asking for is staff—two in my office; two advisers for a minor party. We are a parliamentary party. We are a parliamentary party, and you can't give us the number of staff that is equivalent. The Labor Party have approximately 4.7. We have 0.83 per cent, the lowest in this chamber. All I want is fairness.

Senator PAYMAN (Western Australia—Australia's Voice Whip) (11:28): I rise to express my support for the staffing bill that One Nation have put forward. I think it is outrageous—we are calling on the Prime Minister to stop playing his petty games and to treat us all with the same respect and dignity that we deserve. We were elected by the Australian people. You can hate our politics, you can hate what we do, and you can be annoyed by the fact that I put through so many OPDs and annoy the hell out of your ministers. But I'm holding you to account. You came into government in 2022 talking about transparency, promising the Australian people that you'd be transparent with them, that you'd be upfront and honest. And here we are, as mostly women parliamentarians, asking you—and at times it feels like we're begging you—to get off your high horse and to stop using your discretionary powers to exploit the system.

The additional staff that crossbench senators get is at the discretion of the Prime Minister. For the Australian people who actually don't know about this, the Prime Minister gets to choose how many staff members we get to have. For a parliamentarian, that's one of the most important resources, because we can then service our states and our constituents appropriately. By depriving us of that, he is doing a disservice to the entire state, because of his petty politics. A lot of people I've spoken to—everyday Australians—ask: 'How is that even allowed? You talk a big game, Labor, about 'same job, same pay'. My chief of staff does the same job as the chief of staff of, say, Senator Thorpe or Senator Pocock, and yet she gets paid less. But she has to do a lot more work. They come in early. They leave late. Why? Because the Prime Minister is so bloody petty. Shame on you! Shame on you for doing this to Western Australians.

How dare you claim to stand for women's rights and their welfare and to boast about your female majority caucus when you are stopping women in this place from actually doing their job right. You've got a fat mandate from the Australian people by winning the 2025 election: do bloody better. I hope you're listening, Prime Minister, because I've had it. We've written to your office. We've written to the Special Minister of State, Don Farrell, and we've even FOI'd to see where these documents are going. We follow the bloody processes, and we don't get anything back. You don't even acknowledge that we've sent you these emails and letters.

I can't believe we're still having this conversation. If you are annoyed by the fact that I crossed the floor on a matter of principle, well, you know what, 15 months later you did that same thing. You recognised the State of Palestine, so grow up and just adult, okay? Stop being so petty.

Second Reading
Senator McKENZIE (Victoria—Leader of the Nationals in the Senate) (11:51): I move:
That this bill be now read a second time.
I seek leave to table an explanatory memorandum relating to the bill and the devastating impact of Labor's water buybacks on the Murray-Darling Basin.
Leave granted.
Senator McKENZIE: I table the explanatory memorandum and I seek leave to have the second reading speech incorporated in Hansard.
Leave granted.

The Water Amendment (Ending Further Murray-Darling Basin Water Buybacks) Bill 2026 aims to stop further water buybacks. It stops the Commonwealth from buying more permanent Basin surface water if that purchase would grow the Commonwealth's total share.
It responds to the Government's renewed reliance on permanent water purchases to recover water under the Basin Plan.
And most importantly, it protects irrigators, farmers, and communities from more devastating Commonwealth buybacks destroying the fabric of regional Australia.

Every permanent purchase takes water entitlements out of productive use. Every purchase by the Commonwealth of water distorts the water market and pushes more people who grow our world-class food and fibre out of production. Irrigation communities are already at the end of their tether. They cannot survive another round of Government buybacks.

The need for this Bill has become even more urgent following the Murray-Darling Basin Authority's draft reconciliation of the Sustainable Diversion Limit Adjustment Mechanism and only 22 of the 39 notified projects are expected to be operational by the deadline. Those projects are estimated to deliver around 340 gigalitres of the original 605 gigalitre adjustment, leaving a shortfall of 265 gigalitres.

Basin communities should not be forced to surrender more productive water because governments failed to deliver the infrastructure and environmental projects they promised. The Albanese Government has refused to rule out using further buybacks to make up that shortfall.

Farmers and regional businesses cannot plan, invest or employ people with the constant threat of another round of Commonwealth buybacks hanging over them. This Bill gives them certainty because a failure by government must not become yet another demand for water from farmers.

Buybacks hit the confidence of irrigators, processors and the regional businesses that depend on reliable access to water. They push the price of water up, so that businesses cannot compete in the market for water they need to run their operations.

Productive water underpins food and fibre production and the economic resilience of Basin communities. Most importantly, the loss of productive water to the Commonwealth to meet lofty environmental goals, jeopardises our food security and our national security.

Australians want to eat food grown here, and share what we grow with the rest of the world. We cannot be in a situation where we are importing food from overseas, when we have the best farms and farmers in the world.
This bill amends the Water Act 2007 to prohibit new Commonwealth contracts for permanent or ongoing Basin surface water entitlements where the purchase would increase the Commonwealth's total share.
The Commonwealth already has 72 per cent of the water in the Murray Darling Basin.
The Commonwealth can still manage and rebalance its existing portfolio of water, but it cannot buy more water simply to make up a shortfall.
This will apply to contracts entered into from the day after Royal Assent. Existing contracts are untouched.
It also means that the Commonwealth purchasing water for the Environment Special Account for the 450 gigalitre target becomes expressly subject to the prohibition.
This Bill does not stop any farmer selling an entitlement to another buyer on the market.
Nor does it compel anyone to sell, create any offence or penalty, or reduce any entitlement holder's existing rights.
It also does not alter any right to fair compensation where government action compulsorily acquires, cancels or reduces an entitlement.
It also adds some much needed and important reporting requirements on what water the Commonwealth owns.
The Secretary must report each year on every Commonwealth contract to buy permanent Basin surface water, whether or not it increased the Commonwealth's share.
This report goes to the Minister by 30 September and must be tabled in each House within 15 sitting days.
Reporting covers the full 2026-27 financial year, so Parliament gets a complete account of purchasing this year, including contracts signed before the bill commences.

This Bill aims to regulate how the Commonwealth deals with water. Irrigators and farmers must be completely transparent with their water purchases and water usage. The Commonwealth must meet that same standard.
I commend the Bill to the Senate.

subdebateinfo.title: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026

p.span: Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026
Direction to Committee

The PRESIDENT (12:18): It being past 12.15 pm, pursuant to the order agreed to earlier, there will be a 30-minute debate. The Senate will now proceed to further consideration of the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026 and the motion of Senator Allman-Payne for an instruction to the Committee of the Whole.
Senator RUSTON (South Australia—Deputy Leader of the Opposition in the Senate) (12:18): I seek leave to speak again on the contingency motion that's before the chair.
The PRESIDENT: Leave is granted for 15 minutes.

Senator RUSTON: I stand here today because we will support the government in the bill that is before the chamber, because older Australians cannot wait any longer—not because the problem is fixed, because it is not. Make no mistake about what this is. This is an admission by the government that its assessment system is failing older Australians. For almost 12 months, older Australians and their families, assessors and providers have been telling the government that the computer generated algorithm that has no human override is getting it wrong time and time again. They told the Senate inquiry. They've been telling our electorate offices. They were telling anybody who would listen. And, for almost 12 months, this government told them the system was working. Now, under the weight of sheer evidence, the government has finally capitulated. It has agreed to an independent review of the very algorithm it spent a year defending.

I'll remind the Senate what that evidence looks like. In the full year before the algorithm was put in place, 170 people asked for their assessments to be reviewed. In just the first five months after the algorithm was in place, 834 people asked for a review, and we heard of many more that would have asked for a review but were just so tired of fighting the system.

Australia's peak bodies for geriatric medicine called the tool a clinical safety risk, the Commonwealth Ombudsman launched an investigation, and documents released under freedom of information show the human override was stripped out from the top down, with the department's own staff finding out just days before the system went live.

Then there are the people. A man living with motor neurone disease was told by a computer he needed less help, not more—a cruel progressive terminal illness, and the computer said no. The government has since had to change the rules to recognise motor neurone disease as warranting urgent priority. That is not a refinement; that is an admission the system is getting it wrong. So why support these changes? It's because we've listened. We've listened to stakeholders, to advocates and to older Australians who live with this system every single day. And what they've told us is clear. The system is so bad right now we cannot afford to walk away from even the most modest of improvements. But they told us something else as well. Any improvement of the nature that is being put forward by schedule 4 of this bill must only be interim. It cannot become this government's excuse to stop this process from being fixed. We were not prepared to leave older Australians stuck with the current system while this government takes its time producing a perfect bill that we know will never come. So we've done what stakeholders asked of us. We have supported this improvement, but we've made sure it is interim.

In return for our support, the coalition have received two things. As I said, the first is an independent review of the aged-care assessment tool—a clinically informed review backed by experts in geriatric medicine, dementia care and allied health—examining how the algorithm classifies older Australians and who gets priority. That review must inform the rebuilding of any assessment tool. We're pleased that the government has agreed to it and agreed to publish the results of that review in full so it's there for everybody to see. But a review is not worth the paper it is written on unless its results are turned into action.

Older Australians have had enough waiting under this government, and that is why the second thing we secured matters so much: a sunset clause. These provisions will sunset after 12 months. So the government has 12 months to fix the problems that have been identified by so many people. If it does, older Australians will be better off and we will herald that as a welcome advancement. But if it doesn't, these provisions will lapse and the government will have to come back into this place and explain why it has continued to fail older Australians, why it has failed to give them the care that this government has assessed them as needing. That's our mechanism, and we will force the government to act.

Let me be very clear about one more thing. The coalition is not stepping away from our fight for human override. A computer, and a computer alone, cannot be left to make the decisions about the care needs and care priorities of older Australians. I know the Greens have moved an amendment on human override, and, in principle, we support the Greens. We do not believe that what the government have put forward today is adequate when it comes to human override. What they're putting forward today is an escalation pathway run by the department for people in exceptional circumstances. It is a step—it is an improvement on what we have now—but it is not the same thing as letting a qualified assessor, sitting across the table from an older Australian, correct the computer when it gets it wrong. And we know it is getting it wrong time and time again.

The Senate has already passed the coalition's bill to restore human override, with the support of the Greens and the crossbench, and I acknowledge the incredible support of the crossbench, particularly the Greens and Senator Allman-Payne, on forcing this issue. Earlier this year, a senior minister in the Albanese government told the parliament:
… in every case there needs to be human oversight of any use of AI. We don't just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs…

Well, guess what. We agree with you, Minister. We are simply asking this government to apply that standard to older Australians when it's assessing their care needs and their care need priorities. The government has now said it will review the algorithm, and that is what we expect it to deliver.

We're giving the government the opportunity to go away and do that work. Get it done. But, if it does not, we will be back, and I'm confident that the Greens and the crossbench will be back with us. Together, we have the power to force the government to do the right thing. Remember when Prime Minister Albanese was the opposition leader prior to the 2022 election and told Australians he was going to come in here and put 'the care back into aged care'. Nothing could be further from the reality that older Australians are facing right now. So, today, we're putting the government on notice. The clock is ticking. The coalition will never step away from older Australians. We will never step away from supporting older Australians getting the care they need when they need it. We will keep pushing for a permanent fix, and what we're doing today is telling the government 'you have the chance to come back with a permanent fix, so you'd better do it'.

We will always back a human being able to override a decision when the computer, quite frankly, has made a botch of it. No algorithm has ever grown old. Older Australians deserve a system that sees them as people and not as data. We know, as we stand here today, that 250,000 older Australians are currently waiting to either be assessed or get the package that they've been assessed as needing. We know that, last year, over 6,400 older Australians died while they were waiting to get the home-care package they had been assessed as needing. And we know that right now in excess of 3½ thousand older Australians have been assessed as clinically able to be discharged from our hospitals, yet they languish in hospital beds because this government has rationed care when it comes to aged-care packages. It has failed the sector and the sector's viability with its actions—other actions apart from in this bill—so we're not seeing aged-care beds being built. They need 10½ thousand aged-care beds every year for the next 10 years. Last year, the government's incentives managed to deliver, through the private sector, 802. The government is a long way short of delivering for older Australians, and we believe older Australians need better. That's why we are asking the government to make good on its promise. Fix this absolutely disastrous system. Fix this algorithm that is producing terrible results for older Australians. Quite frankly, older Australians deserve more from their government than they're currently getting.

Senator ALLMAN-PAYNE (Queensland) (12:28): by leave—There's been a lot said in the last 24 hours about the Greens' approach to the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner and Other Measures) Bill 2026. I sat here in the chamber yesterday and listened to numbers of people on the government side accusing the Greens of playing politics with older people.

Let me reassure every older Australian in this country that the Greens will never play politics with older Australians. We have come into this chamber in good faith, seeking to do what advocates are telling us needs to be done and what older people are telling us needs to be done, and that is to try and reinstate human override into the aged-care assessment tool. We came into this chamber in good faith, seeking to split the bill so that the First Nations components of the bill, schedules 1 to 3, could pass through quickly and swiftly, and so that we could have a little bit more time to debate schedule 4 and to seek to reinstate human override—to at least take the fight up to the government to try and get human override back in.

Many government senators spoke yesterday, and many have spoken this morning; they have spoken at great length and quoted many of the advocacy groups that have spoken about this bill. But they have selectively omitted the statement that what people would prefer is that human override be reinstated in aged-care assessments. That is the preference of advocates, carers and providers and of older people themselves. So the Greens have tried to use every lever at our disposal to try and reinstate human override into aged-care assessments. Many government senators have stood in this place, yesterday and this morning, and said that this is 'urgent', and yet have filibustered, delaying us coming to the question of whether we should split the bill and getting on with the committee stage.

I heard many phrases being used by government senators, saying that we only need an escalation pathway because we only need humans to get involved in 'exceptional circumstances'; that we need the algorithm because we need 'consistent, rules based decision-making', or that we need 'a standardised assessment tool'. I kept hearing people talking about 'standardisation'. Senator Ananda-Rajah said that computers are the best decision-makers. Well, I'm sorry, the Greens disagree. People, clinicians, should be the final arbiters of the care that an older person needs to receive—and the government has effectively admitted that by saying that, in some exceptional circumstances, people will have the benefit of a person, a human, a clinician, having the final say. The Greens say that every older person is entitled to have a person make the final decision on the support and the care that they need and should receive.

I put to the government: if you are so concerned about too many clinicians overriding the outcome of the algorithm, then I think that tells you that the algorithm is not working, because if the algorithm were making decisions that accurately reflected the standard and level of care that older people need to receive then there would be very little need to override it. The escalation pathway is an admission that the algorithm is not working, and it is providing human oversight for a small number of people in the aged-care system. Government senators said that we need the algorithm because we need efficient and standardised testing or assessment of older people. Well, again, I put it to you: if the algorithm is so efficient, why do we now have a waitlist of a quarter of a million people waiting either for an assessment or to get the care that they've been assessed as needing? This is efficiency for efficiency's sake.

Senator Whiteaker said that we can't have human override because it would be too expensive. That is precisely why the government is wedded to a computer making these decisions, because this is not a measure to improve the care and support that older people need; this is not a measure to hasten the ability to assess those older people, because we are seeing that assessments are taking longer than ever before. This is a budget measure; it is a measure to cut the cost of care for older Australians. We know this because the government senators said it themselves. As Senator Ruston said, the Greens and the coalition and the remaining members of the crossbench have already voted to reinstate human override into the integrated assessment tool. The Greens have come into this place in good faith seeking to try and get human override back into this bill. We have sought to do it without holding up the First Nations commissioner components of this bill, and we have sought to have a debate in good faith on that question. We have been denied the ability to do that by government senators, who have filibustered for two days so that we could not get to that question. So please don't accuse the Greens of playing politics with older people.

We know that the decisions that are made in this place, as they relate to aged care, are life and death decisions for so many thousands of people. Over 6,000 people in this country died last year waiting for an assessment. That is shameful. And, right the way through this process, we have simply sought to get a better deal for older people—older people who are telling us computers should not be making decisions about their care; older people who are telling us in their thousands that it is unacceptable that, when they finally get assessed, they only get part of their package; and older people who have told us that they are too scared to get an assessment because they know of so many other people who have come back with underassessments from the algorithm and that they're choosing to remain on the Commonwealth Home Support Program because they're terrified that, if they get an assessment, they will be assessed as having a lower level of need than they need. We know this because they have told us. They have told us when they have contacted our offices. They have told us when they have given lived experience evidence at two of our inquiries that have gone right around the country.

I fail to understand how the department and the government can continue to be so wedded to the idea that a computer is the best decision-maker for the care needs of older people. We know their needs are complex. No two older people are the same. No two older people's houses and the way they're laid out are the same. No two older people's support systems, whether they have family and who has what amount of time, are the same. None of us would want to go into a hospital and have a doctor tell us that they're just going to punch our condition or our symptoms into a computer and that it'll tell us what they're going to do, and, if we don't agree with it, too bad, wait for a review that could take 90 days. Older people don't have time to wait. In so many instances, they don't want to ask for help until they absolutely need it. Providers and carers and their families tell us that. When an older person reaches out to seek help and support in aged care, it's because they really need it—and they need it now. Not in six months time, when they might be able to get an assessment; not in another 12 months time, when they might be able to get a package—they need it now.

These reforms are failing older people. You cannot say that the reforms are on the right track when waitlists are blowing out, when people are telling us that they are not getting the care that they need and when they can't even get a full package when it's finally assigned. That is not a system that works well. Older people saying that they can't afford co-payments and that they're going without care is not a system that is working well. The Greens have said that we won't stand in the way of this bill going through to appoint the First Nations commissioner, and we won't stand in the way of the bill going through if our amendments aren't successful. We know that older people need as many avenues as possible to access the right type of care at the time that they need it.

But I can't help reflect that this is a missed opportunity. As Senator Ruston said, the Greens, the coalition and the crossbench have worked together to pressure the government. We had an opportunity here to try again to reinsert human override into this bill, to force the government to take another look at it and to keep the pressure on them. Saying that you're going to do a review that was needed 12 months ago, because it was obvious from the beginning that this algorithm is not working, is such a small step forward. It just makes more older people wait. Everything that happens around older people is just about waiting. 'Wait for us to do another review. Wait for us to see whether it makes the algorithm any better. Wait to see if we need to tinker around the edges a little bit more.' All the while, a quarter-of-a-million people are waiting for care and dying while they wait. I am incredibly disappointed that we were not able to work with other members of this chamber to keep the pressure on, to force them to at least reject putting human override in again, because that is what is needed here.

Every older person in this country deserves to have a person have the final say on the care that they need. And families should not have to be in a situation where they see their older parent or their grandparent die waiting for care. I know what that feels like. I watched my mum die of MND like so many other people do in this country, knowing how rejected they felt that the government did not care enough to give them the care that they needed when they desperately needed it. I watched my father, a man in his late 70s, trying to do his very best to care for her without any package support at all. And I know that the MND community welcomes the rapid access, but I want to put on the record again that it is still far too little. When it costs $300,000 a year to care for somebody in the late stages of MND, and the most they can get is $70,000, if the algorithm gets it right, that is not okay. No family in this country should have to be trying to fight their way through a system that is so complex and so complicated, only to find themselves in a situation where they feel like they have to fight for their older parent or family member to get the care they need because a computer is making those decisions and getting them wrong. It's already hard enough to navigate the system.

My plea to everyone in this chamber is this. We have lost an opportunity on this bill to put humans back in charge of making the decisions for older people's care. But I hope the next time we have a piece of legislation before us that gives us the opportunity to do that, we can get it done, because older people do not have time to wait.

Senator LIDDLE (South Australia—Deputy Opposition Whip in the Senate) (12:43): I rise to speak on the Aged Care Legislation Amendment (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner) and Other Measures Bill 2026. The coalition welcomes the commissioner, and I have said so in this place earlier this week. Today I want to speak about the government's changes to aged-care assessment and why the coalition will support them. Let me be clear at the outset. We are supporting the changes in this bill because older Australians cannot afford to wait any longer. They can't afford to wait any longer. They're telling us that right around the country, when you listen to them and you listen to their families. The problem is not fixed. It is absolutely not fixed. Make no mistake about what this is: an admission by the government that its assessment system is failing older Australians. For almost 12 months, older Australians, their families, assessors and providers have been telling this government that the algorithm is getting it wrong. They told the Senate inquiry. They told our electorate offices. They told anyone who would listen. For almost 12 months, this government told them the system was working.

Now, under the sheer weight of evidence, the government, which talks about caring for vulnerable people, has finally capitulated. It has agreed to an independent review of the very algorithm it spent a year defending. I'm not sure how you could defend it with the weight of evidence that said the algorithm was just the wrong thing to do. It wasn't assessing people appropriately. It was unfair. It was making mistakes. There was the removal of human override. How much more wrong can you get it?

We are giving the government the opportunity to go away, do that work and get it done, but if it does not, we will be back, and I'm confident the Greens and the crossbench will be with us. Together, we will force this government to do the right thing. The coalition won't step away from this fight for human override. That's because we have heard it time and time again. Senator Ruston and I have been speaking to people in communities across South Australia and everywhere else in this country, and we're hearing exactly the same message. The only people that don't seem to be hearing that are on the opposite side. We won't move one inch from pushing for this to happen.

I know the Greens have moved an amendment on human override. We do not believe what the government has put forward is adequate when it comes to human override. An escalation pathway run by the department for people in exceptional circumstances is a step, but it is not the same as letting a qualified assessor sit across the table from an older Australian and correct the computer when it gets it wrong. This Senate has already passed the coalition's bill to restore human override with the support of the Greens and the crossbench. Earlier this year, a senior minister in this government told the parliament:
… in every case there needs to be human oversight of any use of AI. We don't just hand over decision-making to abstract computer programs …

Of course the coalition agrees; it's common sense. Today, we are putting this government on notice. The clock is ticking. The coalition will never step away from older Australians. We will keep pushing for a permanent fix, and we will always back human override, because no algorithm has ever grown old. Every Australian is different, and older Australians deserve a system that sees them as people, not as data. They deserve nothing less.

subdebateinfo.title: Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation) Bill 2026

p.span: Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation) Bill 2026
Second Reading
Consideration resumed of the motion:
That this bill be now read a second time.
Senator HENDERSON (Victoria) (12:48): I move:
At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate:

(a) affirms that reliable and affordable mobile coverage is an essential service for regional, rural and remote Australians, underpinning personal safety, business productivity and participation in the digital economy; and
(b) is of the opinion that the bill:

(i) does not provide sufficient certainty that universal outdoor mobile connectivity for voice and SMS services will be delivered to all Australians within the requisite timeframe, particularly for those living in regional, rural and remote Australia,
(ii) places a vague and uncertain obligation on carriers and carriage service providers to provide 'reasonable access' to outdoor mobile connectivity on an 'equitable basis',

(iii) legislates the use of technologies such as voice to satellite before it either exists at scale or is commercially available, fuelling uncertainty and raising false hope, particularly for Australians living or working in regional Australia,
(iv) does not account for the fact that many handset devices in the Australian market will not be compatible with the technology required to access universal outdoor mobile connectivity, and
(v) does not include express obligations in relation to universal access to triple zero emergency voice calls and SMS messages which is crucial for the health and safety of all Australians; and
(c) notes that:

(i) the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission commenced an inquiry on 5 August 2026 into regional mobile coverage across Australia, including whether one or more wholesale mobile services, including domestic roaming, should be declared, and that this inquiry provides the appropriate forum to assess the feasibility of a regional mobile roaming service, and

(ii) the Universal Service Obligation, which was designed to ensure reasonable and equitable access to a standard telephone service and payphones, is no longer fit for purpose and should be modernised to establish stronger expectations on carriers and carriage service providers to deliver reliable mobile and internet services, particularly in regional, rural and remote Australia".

The coalition supports the objective of improving connectivity for regional Australians, but aspirations are no substitute for implementation. The Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation) Bill 2026 is big on motherhood statements but, regrettably, has very little substance. And let's not forget the context. This so-called Labor promise to deliver universal outdoor mobile communications was made in February 2025 in the lead-up to the last federal election. This was all about the politics devised by the office of the previous minister for communications, Ms Rowland, to cover up the fact that Labor was planning to axe vital funding for regional communications.

That is exactly what happened in the May budget this year, to the great shame of the Albanese government. This government has turned its back on the regions by slashing vital programs to support regional connectivity, including the Mobile Black Spot Program. The communications minister even made the heartless decision to axe the Regional Tech Hub, another coalition initiative which has played such a valuable role in supporting regional Australians with their internet and phone connectivity challenges.

While the intent of the bill is broadly supported by the mobile network operators and key stakeholders, the government has very significantly failed to address how universal mobile coverage for text messages and voice calls can possibly be delivered by the commencement date of 1 December 2027. That is because the technology does not currently exist. The satellites are not in the sky, satellite compatible devices are not available at scale, and the mobile satellite spectrum has not been allocated. While Telstra may have a deal in place with SpaceX to, by the end of next year, deliver text and voice mobile communications via Starlink's low Earth orbit satellite, Optus and TPG have made clear that this is not achievable in the timeframe available. In fact, it may not be possible for TPG and Optus to deliver this technology until maybe 2029 or even 2030 and beyond. This is a bill that is big on promises and very short on delivery.

But, as they say, never let the facts get in the way of the story. Despite this bill being riddled with uncertainty, Minister Wells, when it was introduced into the House and passed in the House, posted a video on social media saying that 'the legislation delivers better service wherever you can see the sky'. It's completely wrong—completely misleading; we didn't hear from the Ooshies, but we've had another social media video from the minister which is just utter nonsense. The problem is that the government has put up the 'open for business' sign before the shop has even been built. Australians can look to the sky all they like; until the direct-to-device satellites are in place, the technology is proven and the commercial agreements with Australia's mobile network operators are done, there is no universal service to deliver. A slogan is not coverage, a promise is not a mobile service, and looking at the sky will not make your phone work. As I say, this bill is big on promises, big on talk and very, very small on delivery.

I will go through some of the components of the bill. But we have, of course, proposed a number of amendments, and I am hoping that the Senate will support those amendments. These will try and fill in some of the very significant gaps with this bill. The first one relates to temporary disaster roaming, which currently is only a voluntary scheme. We don't believe that that is good enough. The government has talked about temporary disaster roaming for a number of years. The technology has been tested, the need is obvious, yet there is only a voluntary scheme in place. We're told that it commenced as of 1 October. This amendment draws a line in the sand. It makes it clear that, to the extent that the voluntary scheme is not in place or it falters, the minister must act and establish a framework commencing no later than 1 December. We believe that it's unacceptable—when lives depend on access to communications during a bushfire, flood or cyclone or other disasters and Australians need access to disaster roaming—and a very significant misstep that the minister put in place a voluntary scheme rather than legislating for temporary disaster roaming. So we are very hopeful that this important amendment will be supported by the Senate.

We have also proposed an amendment relating to the minister being required to make standards for the performance and reliability of mobile networks. The government has talked endlessly about coverage, but coverage means nothing if the service is unreliable, congested or simply does not work. This bill, unfortunately, just gives the minister discretion to set standards, and we think that that is insufficient. Australians need accountability from mobile networks, which are becoming more and more crucial. So this amendment requires the minister to establish minimum standards for terrestrial mobile networks, informed by the ACCC's current inquiry and developed with regulators, carriers and consumers. Australians should not have to accept dropped calls, unusable data and persistent black spots as normal.

This is also in the context of the fact that, despite the recommendation in the Bean review that the triple zero regulatory framework should be reviewed and updated—because we've seen some catastrophic outages, including, of course, in relation to the vital triple zero service—the government sat on its hands for two years. That is simply not good enough, so we believe that there must be a requirement for these standards to be made. What is very significant as part of this work is the ACCC's inquiry, and I'll come to that in a moment.

The other amendment relates to mobile roaming. The government has turned its back on mobile roaming, and there is very good cause to consider how we can improve connectivity in the regions, including through mobile roaming. Since our bill inquiry, which we conducted through the Environment and Communications Legislation Committee, what has been very significant is the announcement by the ACCC of an inquiry to examine regional mobile coverage across Australia and whether regulating wholesale access to some mobile services could improve consumer outcomes. This inquiry will examine a lot of these issues, including mobile roaming. There have been a number of different inquiries. Back in 2017, the ACCC decided against mobile roaming, but in recent years we have seen investment by the telcos in the regions decline, and that is also the observation of the ACCC. So this is very significant, and this work cannot be ignored. That is why, as part of making the performance and reliability standards, the minister needs to take this very substantial inquiry and its findings into account.

This inquiry, I think, is a game changer, and the telcos are on notice because, of course, the ACCC has the ability to compel the production of documents that we can't access because they are commercial-in-confidence. We have sought, for instance, the investment pipeline of the telcos to understand what their investment plans are for regional Australia, and those documents have been denied. So the ACCC's work in this respect is very significant, and it will also, I think, play a very important role in the fact that there is just not enough regulation surrounding mobile networks in this country, which have become completely vital to every Australian. More and more Australians are dropping off their landline and relying on their mobile phone and on connectivity. So, as I say, we cannot overstate the importance of the ACCC inquiry, which I think will hold the government to account for its failure to take these issues seriously enough.

I want to address a couple of specific issues with this bill in more detail. As I say, it is incredibly alarming that the government has slashed and burned regional connectivity funding as if the regions don't matter anymore, because mobile roaming is not going to work if there is no connectivity at all. There are still many parts of this country where large regional communities either have access to deficient connectivity or have no mobile connectivity, and that has been made worse by the government's botched 3G shutdown, which has actually reduced coverage in some parts of regional Australia.

So the fact that the minister is bringing forward a bill, which has got big aspirations but very little meat on the bones, and is pretending that almost everything's fine because we now have this whole new world of satellite connectivity where we can hold our phone, look to the sky and think everything's going to be great is complete rubbish, as I've set out, because the technology is not yet available. What's made this even more deceptive is that the government has heavily promoted the commencement date of 1 December 2027 when it knows—and it is on notice—that two of the three telcos will not be able to deliver within that timeframe because the technology simply does not exist.

Another concern I want to raise is that there are a lot of 'get out of jail' clauses here. The bill leaves far too much to be decided later by the minister, by way of a general power to make determinations, and critical concepts such as 'reasonably available' and 'equitable basis' are left undefined. There are very uncertain obligations on providing mobile connectivity that's reasonably available on an equitable basis. This means that the parliament is being asked to pass the framework now and trust the minister to write much of the substance down the track. That is also very concerning.

The other really concerning issue with this bill is spectrum. Direct-to-device satellite services depend on access to a suitable radio frequency spectrum, yet the bill has not resolved how that spectrum will be secured, allocated or managed alongside existing terrestrial mobile services. The Senate inquiry heard all sorts of serious warnings from industry. Optus said satellite services could require carriers to cannibalise spectrum currently used for terrestrial mobile networks. This, of course, is a matter currently with ACMA, but how can a bill be put forward with such definitive requirements while really critical issues such as spectrum are still not determined?

The other major problem, of course, is that this connectivity proposed to be in place by 1 December next year depends on device compatibility. We heard in our inquiry that many existing handsets will not support the full direct-to-device satellite service compatibility that is required. That is a real issue, of course, when Australians are being told that everything will be fine by the end of next year but they are then required to upgrade their phones.

The amendments that we have brought forward, which we hope will be supported by the Senate, expose essential weakness with this bill. We support the intent of the bill, but the government has got to do much better. I say shame on the government for their disgraceful cuts to regional connectivity. (Time expired)

Senator HANSON-YOUNG (South Australia—Manager of Australian Greens Business in the Senate) (13:03): I rise to contribute to the debate on the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation) Bill 2026 today. I want to put it clearly on the record from the beginning that this is a missed opportunity for the government to work with the parliament to fix Australia's broken telecommunications laws. They are simply not up to scratch. They are not working and they are failing millions and millions of Australians. Australia's telecommunications laws are virtually silent on the need for mobile service to be reliable, to be guaranteed and to have some basic elements of standards. Unlike landline services—you see those old phones plugged into the wall which of course have had, for many, many years, rules and regulations about how reliable those services should be—there is virtually nothing in law that says mobile phone companies must provide a reliable and working service to their customers. And yet Australians across the board now use mobile phones far more than they use landlines. There are millions of households across Australia that don't even have a landline anymore and use their mobile phone service as their only form of telecommunication.

Our laws are not up to scratch. They're not fit for purpose, they're out of date, and they need to be fixed. There would have been an opportunity, in this piece of legislation—with proper negotiations, talk and a willingness across all sides of this chamber—to actually do something to improve the level of standard and reliability for Australians. But that's not what we've got here. We've got a bill that is really the bare basics and goes nowhere near lifting the level of standards and guaranteed reliability that Australians should expect and do deserve from their mobile phone carriers.

Why is it that we're debating a bill today that doesn't give proper regulations for working mobile phone services? It's because the mobile phone companies don't want these rules. The mobile phone companies, the big telcos— Telstra, Optus and TPG—are very happy not to have rules and regulations that say they must provide a service to their customers so that when somebody signs up for a mobile phone contract that it might actually work and that, if it doesn't work, customers should be entitled to some compensation. If you've bought a product, if you've signed a contract and then it doesn't work, if it costs your business money and it costs you time, and if you've suffered as a result of your mobile phone not working, you should be able to seek compensation. But there's nothing like that in Australian law.

The Greens are moving amendments today that would put that type of compensation in law so that Australians can rely on having a working mobile phone and the companies are held to account if indeed the phone service goes down. We have seen hundreds—in fact, there have been thousands—of outages of the mobile phone network in the last year. We know millions and millions of Australians have been impacted in the last year because their mobile phone didn't work. This has been because the big telcos have been too busy looking after themselves, putting their profits first and not investing in reliable infrastructure. Because there are no laws that require them to offer some guarantees about the reliability of their service, they get away with it. Because there are no laws that say they should pay if their service goes down and it costs their customers money, they get away with it. The big outage that happened in July—when millions of Australians were left in the cold with dead mobile phones, locked out of public transport, locked out of trading in their small businesses, not able to use their emergency distress buttons and not able to call triple zero—was because Telstra's system went down. Do you know how much that cost the Australian economy? It cost $552 million. Australians are paying the price because the big telcos think they can keep getting away with a dodgy service.

I must say I'm a bit frustrated that we're in here today. We're about to ram through this bill, and it doesn't actually go to the heart of the problem. It doesn't matter how much spin the big telcos, the minister's office, the government or anybody else puts on it, this bill is going to pass and Australians have no more protection or guarantees that their mobile phone service will work. I guarantee there will continue to be outages. There will continue to be failures of triple zero calls. The worst thing of all is what happens if you can't call triple zero. What happens? Well, we know. Sadly, we've seen people lose their lives because the mobile phone companies were too busy putting their profits ahead of people's safety. We had an opportunity to fix that in here today. This bill doesn't do it.

I'll be moving a series of amendments that go to this point, saying that it should be a law that, if you provide a mobile phone service, it should work. It should be the law that, if your mobile phone service—Telstra, Optus, TPG, Vodafone—fails, you should pay for that. The Australian people and taxpayers shouldn't be covering the cost. We'll put in place an amendment in this chamber soon and put to this chamber the opportunity for the government and the opposition to vote for domestic roaming. Why is it that, in other countries around the world, people can swap from mobile phone company to mobile phone company based on being able to access a working service, yet, in Australia, Australians are locked out of that. It is just not right. The big telcos are laughing all the way to the bank. They're clocking up their profits, yet the service that they provide is crap. It's unreliable, it's dangerous, and it's costing people their businesses and lives. We should have fixed it. It should have been done in this bill. I think it is appalling that the pressure that the big telcos have put on both the Labor Party and the coalition means they've failed to do it in this bill—gutless, gutless, gutless.

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH (Victoria) (13:11): I rise to speak on the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment (Universal Outdoor Mobile Obligation) Bill 2026. Connectivity is critical infrastructure. We take it for granted, but, when it breaks down, it can have devastating consequences. This was best seen during the fires that affected Victoria in January, which were amongst the worst natural disasters in Victoria's history. These summer fires burned through 440,000 hectares, including more than 144,000 hectares in the Longwood region, a region that I had the privilege and opportunity to visit. This event had the largest agricultural impact from fire in Victoria's history. There were 451 homes lost, with over 1,110 outhouses lost and 45,000 livestock losses. The shire of Murrindindi, in particular, was worst affected, but it also affected the shires of Mitchell, Mansfield and Strathbogie. It took the life of one Mansfield resident, cattle farmer Mr Max Hobson.

I want to describe the losses in Murrindindi because they speak to what this community had to go through and how they had to respond and recover when communications collapsed. That is the backdrop against the significance of having universal outdoor mobile coverage. This bill will enable communication, initially by text messaging, to happen anywhere you can see the sky. I can't tell you how critical that is, but you need to understand the losses this community experienced. In Murrindindi, nearly 200 homes were destroyed along with over 400 sheds and outhouses. There were 1,157 properties impacted. There were nearly 7,800 livestock losses, constituting $20 million in losses—5,600 sheep, over 1,500 cattle and nearly 500 beehives as well as poultry, goats, three horses, one pig and 40 other animals. Over 4,800 kilometres of fencing was destroyed, costing over $120 million to replace. I note that many farms were underinsured for fencing, plants and other infrastructure. And, of course, there were impacts on the natural environment. An estimated 1,200 to 1,400 tree hollows were lost, affecting and impacting threatened species, like gang-gang cockatoos, powerful owls and yellow-tailed black cockatoos, which I see frequently when I travel to that region.

During these catastrophic conditions, comms failed entirely, hampering the response and recovery of this community. According to Telstra—and this came from the Victorian state government inquiry that happened shortly after—270 fixed and mobile sites went offline. With the fire starting on 7 January, some four days later, as many as 25 communities were identified as being at risk of losing all mobile and broadband services. Imagine that. Courageous local emergency services were forced to relocate from their state-of-the-art relatively new facility in Alexandra to Seymour because the comms failed. They had to keep fighting without mobile connection. Can you imagine that? Crews lost communication. Even digital radios that were relatively new on the CFA trucks failed because they did not work in black spots, leaving these crews vulnerable and unable to contact each other and unable to communicate with their incident controllers. I can't imagine the circumstances of this.

In the recovery phase, I spoke to one farmer who described what it was like. In searing heat, he had to bury carcases of his stock. In the midst of this, he had to get approval, and he had to use physical runners to send forms to the local state authorities to get permission to bury his stock, in searing heat, because the comms failed. Under this law, as I said before, you will be able to get outdoor coverage via text messaging initially nearly anywhere if you can look up to see the sky. It could be a game changer, if we have another terrible fire season, as is being predicted. It will be enabled by LEO satellites. From as early as 1 December 2027, this law requires Telstra, Optus and TPG to provide baseline outdoor coverage across Australia where reasonably possible, using their towers together with these low-Earth-orbit, or LEO, satellites.

As of the beginning of this month, Telstra, Optus and TPG will activate temporary disaster roaming so that, when one network goes down during a severe weather event, customers can automatically be camped onto another network without losing service. Combined with UOMO, this provides options; it provides layers of safeguards so that, when the chips are down, if comms fails, people have options. I hope we never again have to go through the kind of catastrophe and stress and anxiety that the community of Victoria, particularly in Murrindindi, experienced.

I'd like to thank those firefighters, the CFA volunteers, the emergency personnel, the local leaders and the community members who welcomed me and share their stories and who have enabled this bill to come to pass. I commend this bill to the Senate.
