At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate:

(a) affirms that reliable and affordable mobile coverage is an essential service for regional, rural and remote Australians, underpinning personal safety, business productivity and participation in the digital economy; and
(b) is of the opinion that the bill:

(i) does not provide sufficient certainty that universal outdoor mobile connectivity for voice and SMS services will be delivered to all Australians within the requisite timeframe, particularly for those living in regional, rural and remote Australia,
(ii) places a vague and uncertain obligation on carriers and carriage service providers to provide 'reasonable access' to outdoor mobile connectivity on an 'equitable basis',

(iii) legislates the use of technologies such as voice to satellite before it either exists at scale or is commercially available, fuelling uncertainty and raising false hope, particularly for Australians living or working in regional Australia,
(iv) does not account for the fact that many handset devices in the Australian market will not be compatible with the technology required to access universal outdoor mobile connectivity, and
(v) does not include express obligations in relation to universal access to triple zero emergency voice calls and SMS messages which is crucial for the health and safety of all Australians; and
(c) notes that:

(i) the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission commenced an inquiry on 5 August 2026 into regional mobile coverage across Australia, including whether one or more wholesale mobile services, including domestic roaming, should be declared, and that this inquiry provides the appropriate forum to assess the feasibility of a regional mobile roaming service, and

(ii) the Universal Service Obligation, which was designed to ensure reasonable and equitable access to a standard telephone service and payphones, is no longer fit for purpose and should be modernised to establish stronger expectations on carriers and carriage service providers to deliver reliable mobile and internet services, particularly in regional, rural and remote Australia".

Senator Colbeck: I have a point of order on direct relevance. It was a very tight question. I wanted to know how much of the $4.4 billion revenue comes from small businesses, including farm businesses.

Senator McKenzie: Great question.

Trade with the European Union

Senator CICCONE (Victoria) (14:53): Happy Thursday, President. I've got a great question before me today, and I'd love to ask my question to my very good friend the Minister for Trade and Tourism, the wonderful Senator Farrell. In March, the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese—
Senator McKenzie: Trying to sell the EU agreement?
Senator CICCONE: listen up, Senator McKenzie—and the President of the European Union announced—
The PRESIDENT: Senator Ciccone—
Senator CICCONE: through you—

The PRESIDENT: please resume your seat. Senator Mckenzie, I've tried a number of different strategies today, including humour, which clearly have all failed. If you can't be quiet, leave the chamber. Senator CICCONE: As I was saying: Minister, in March, the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, and the President of the European Union announced that Australia and the EU had concluded negotiations on a new free trade agreement. It will give Australian businesses access to hundreds of millions of consumers across 27 countries and to an economy worth trillions of dollars. In practical terms, it's not just one market; it's 27 new markets, each with different tastes and opportunities for Australian producers. From its entry into force, nearly 98 per cent of Australian exports to the EU will enter tariff free, delivering benefits worth billions of dollars in the first year alone. By removing prohibitive trade barriers, the agreement will create major opportunities for South Australian fishers, Queensland pineapple growers, New South Wales sheep farmers, Victorian prosecco producers and many, many more. Senator Canavan, for instance, is trying to lead the Liberal Party away from free trade and straight into an economic dead end. He is promising an economy that exists only in their imagination, all to try and save his own political skin. Thankfully, many senators, including some of those opposite, understand that more trade means more opportunity for Australia, especially in the regions. I look forward to working with anyone—

Cybersafety

Senator BELL (New South Wales—One Nation Whip) (15:00): My question is to the Minister representing the Minister for Communications, Senator Farrell. At the National Press Club today, Minister Wells insisted Labor's new digital duty of care bill would not be used for surveillance to restrict free speech or target political opinions. Senator FARRELL (South Australia—Minister for Trade and Tourism, Special Minister of State and Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate) (15:00): I thank Senator Bell for his question. Our digital duty of care will set basic safety standards for the digital services that we use every day, just like we have for food, for cars and for kids toys. It will provide Australians over the age of 16 with agency over their algorithms. Social media companies will have to offer genuine choice and respect that choice or face significant competition. Our laws will let Australians decide for themselves what they see. So, I think, in fundamental terms, Senator Bell, we would disagree with your characterisation of what the government is doing here. Right now, foreign companies make those choices for you, and they make them without asking. People will still be able to see recommended content if they want to, but they'll also have the option to just see friends and creators that they choose. Parliament should support giving more choice and more control, and I would encourage One Nation to do exactly that.
The PRESIDENT: Senator bell, first supplementary?

Senator BELL (New South Wales—One Nation Whip) (15:02): Minister, why is Labor giving the eSafety Commissioner these covert powers without requiring detailed independent oversight of what information is collected, and how is it used? What is the government trying to cover up?

Senator STEWART (Victoria) (15:03): My question is to the Minister for Indigenous Australians, Senator McCarthy. Senator McCARTHY (Northern Territory—Minister for Indigenous Australians) (15:04): I thank Senator Stewart for the question. I know she's a fierce advocate for Indigenous businesses. I can tell the Senate there are more than 13,000 First Nations businesses around the country. They're generating more than $16 billion in revenue. They're paying $4.2 billion in wages and employing over 116,000 people in the economy, and I can tell you the Albanese Labor government is supporting them every step of the way. It's this government that has strengthened the Indigenous Procurement Policy, which is driving government purchasing towards First Nations businesses and supporting economic empowerment for individuals, families and communities.

And we're backing First Nations women in business, too. Our new business coaching program, delivered by Indigenous Business Australia, is providing tailored coaching, mentoring and business capability development opportunities for First Nations women. This program is supporting First Nations women to turn business ideas into successful new enterprises. And there's more. We've made a $20.5 million investment in Indigenous business and employment hubs, and these hubs are located in Sydney, Perth, Adelaide, Hobart, Darwin and Alice Springs. The hubs offer First Nations businesses and entrepreneurs tailored support to help them and their businesses thrive. October might be Indigenous Business Month, but the Albanese Labor government backs Indigenous businesses all year round.
The PRESIDENT: Senator Stewart, first supplementary?

Senator STEWART (Victoria) (15:06): Thank you, Minister. The Albanese Labor government's Indigenous business hubs are providing on-the-ground assistance for Indigenous businesses to thrive. What has been the feedback about the experiences of businesses who are using those hubs?

Senator Hume: Not if they're in trusts.
The PRESIDENT: Order! Do you think we could just have one set of questions and answers without the constant interjection? Let's try really hard. Senator Stewart, second supplementary?

Senator STEWART (Victoria) (15:07): The Albanese Labor government is achieving results with business hubs and the Indigenous Procurement Policy. Are there any obstacles standing in the way of the government's approach to economic empowerment for First Nations people?

Senator McCARTHY (Northern Territory—Minister for Indigenous Australians) (15:07): Thank you, Senator. Yes, there certainly are. The Albanese Labor government will always celebrate the achievements of First Nations people and work with them, whether it's in business, in the arts or in education, and we'll back that success with investment and support, like our women-in-business program, our strengthening of the Indigenous Procurement Policy and our business hubs. These are investments that are having a real impact on the lives of First Nations people. Those opposite are very good at identifying a problem, and we never hear a solution from them. In fact, we've been accused of being too ambitious and not having enough ambition. Their entire policy offering for First Nations people at the last election was about whether they would stand in front of an Aboriginal flag: One flag? Three flags? That was their policy. While they try to out 'One Nation' One Nation, we're getting on with improving the lives of First Nations people in this country.

( Senator O'Sullivan ) (15:16): With the concurrence of the Senate, the clerks will set the clocks in accordance with informal arrangements agreed by the whips.
Senator DUNIAM (Tasmania—Manager of Opposition Business in the Senate) (15:16): I move:
That the Senate take note of the answers given by ministers to questions without notice asked by Opposition senators today

In doing so, can I say: what a terrible way for me to end my Senate career—to hear these terrible answers about how out of touch this government is with real people, small businesses and farmers. Apparently this government doesn't know what a farmer is, by the way. We sort of had to stumble through question time there, trying to figure out how this government felt.
Senator Wong: Hey, hey, hey, my grandfather's a farmer.

Senator DUNIAM: Oh, well, the grandfather of Senator Wong, the Leader of the Government in the Senate, is a farmer, so we'll take that. But, of course, when the question was asked, 'Where does food come from?' they all said Uber Eats.

What really did astound me out of that set of questions and the answers given was, of course, the response to the question about McPhillamys goldmine. In the last term, I was the shadow environment minister, and, on this issue, the finding of the government—the former environment minister Ms Plibersek—was to rule against the capacity for this billion-dollar goldmine to proceed—a mine, I might say, that met every state and federal planning and environment approval and had gone through millions of dollars of assessments and years of work. It had done the work with the traditional owner group, the Orange Local Aboriginal Land Council, only to be stopped by Minister Plibersek, the minister who also gave it environmental approval. The same minister, after all of those approvals had been given, then took in a bit of evidence from a group who didn't actually represent the traditional owners of that part of the country around Orange, Bathurst and Blayney, which the McPhillamys goldmine was located in. After all of that work, the minister said, 'No, it cannot proceed,' because of evidence we have never seen—evidence that was provided in secret by a group of people who, again did not represent the traditional owners, evidence that has never been tendered to the proponents of the mine to analyse, and evidence that was perhaps given orally. It's not even required under the act that governs this that it be given in written form.

So how is this piece of legislation, which is, in fact, as old as me, still fit for purpose? This government has an opportunity to reform it, and I believe a test that the new legislation should pass is: would this mine survive under the new laws? If the answer is yes then pass the laws. If the answer is no then go back to the drawing board. It's pretty simple.

The fact is that we have people who want to invest in this country and this government's mantra is: 'We want a future made in Australia. We want to create more jobs. We want to get the economy ticking over.' Well, how do you do that when you have a government that allows someone, whether they're a domestic investor or a foreign investor who has come to this country, to sink money into multiple approval processes over a long period of time, only to say, at the very last hurdle: 'You know what? We're not going to let you go through with this. We're not going to tell you why. Good luck. Hope you do well'?

The court, of course, found, just yesterday—and it was a great gift for me, on the day of my valedictory speech to this Senate, which I'm now going past and now talking again, to have the court recognise this—that this government made a terrible decision by denying procedural fairness to the proponents by hiding the evidence they relied on from the proponents of the mine. So I hope this government takes this opportunity to reflect on how terrible this decision was and how, if they are really interested in a future made in Australia, they'll get these laws right. In saying that, it's been a real delight to sit through my last question time as a senator for Tasmania, and I thank my colleagues again for their good humour and forbearance with me as I fill in that five-minute slot.

The ACTING DEPUTY PRESIDENT
( Senator O'Sullivan ): Senator Duniam, may I say, that was a very fitting conclusion to your time in the chamber, although we will have you for estimates. So I look forward to your continuing contribution in the Senate.

p.span: Senator WALKER (South Australia) (15:20): I also congratulate Senator Duniam on his last contribution in this place. Our changes at its core are about making the system fairer for working Australians. At the core of our reforms to trusts is aligning the treatment of income from assets and income from work and helping fund our tax cuts to Australian workers. It is true that the flexibility provided by trusts can also allow some Australians to plan their tax affairs in ways that aren't available to most workers and their families. To make Australia a fairer country, we need to make sure that tax obligations are distributed evenly throughout our society.

Those in this chamber know that numerous reviews have raised concerns with tax arrangements for discretionary trusts over many years. The first instance of this was a report in 1975. There was the Ralph review in 1999. There was the Henry review. And there was the coalition's own tax discussion paper in 2015, which I know is a pretty inconvenient truth for those opposite. The settings are becoming more unsustainable with the number of discretionary trusts doubling over the past 20 years to over 800,000. There are legitimate reasons to use trusts, and anyone operating through discretionary trusts can continue to do so. There is a substantial period for anyone using a trust to prepare before the 1 July 2028 start date, and we're providing expanded options to limit or eliminate restructuring costs as well. That includes expanded rollover relief from 2027 and options for trusts to elect to be exempt without requiring a restructure or paying a wage to beneficiaries employed in the trust.

The majority of trust income flows to the top earning 10 per cent of Australian families. About 90 per cent of the total private trust wealth is held by 10 per cent of households. The vast majority of Australians do not receive a discretionary trust income, and the vast majority of small businesses also do not operate using a trust. Less than 10 per cent of small businesses will be affected in any given year. This change is about improving the fairness, integrity and sustainability of the tax system. We're focused on taking the pressure off Australians with permanent cost-of-living relief, including tax cuts for every Australian taxpayer that started on 1 July this year. Those opposite are determined to present these fairer tax changes as an attack on business. We in the Labor Party see it for what it is: a smoke screen that they can hide behind while trying to protect their ability to minimise their tax and increase the divide.

Like I've already touched on, our reforms are about better aligning the tax treatment of incomes from assets and income from work and to help fund tax cuts for Australian workers. It's also worth noting that primary production income is exempt from the minimum tax on trusts, which we announced on budget night. It's also important that we note that this week the National Farmers' Federation said:
We strongly welcome the Government's decision to legislate the exemption for primary production income, providing critical certainty for farming families.

Senator KOVACIC (New South Wales) (15:24): Do you know an inconvenient truth? I'll tell you an inconvenient truth. This government has trashed the economy, this government has crushed Australian households and this government has brought Australian small businesses to their knees. That's the inconvenient truth. The answers, or the lack of answers, that we got to the questions asked about trusts are very telling. The suggestion that this is a niche group of businesses at the top end of the town is absolutely false. This is the everyday tradie. This is a builder, someone in the construction industry. It also crosses into other service industries like hairdressers and doctors and dentists—you name it. Do you know what they all have in common? They're all small businesses. They're not large businesses. They're not multinationals. They're Australian small businesses that have been targeted by this Albanese Labor government with even more tax.

One of the answers that Minister Wong gave was in relation to it just being about a small group of businesses or individuals that receive their income via a trust. I'll take a step back. We are in a housing crisis. We don't have enough houses. That's a given. In the budget in May, instead of making it easier for young Australians to get into a home, this government decided to increase taxes across a whole spectrum of mechanisms under the shield of intergenerational equity. We all know that to be false. They said that these taxes would make it easier for young Australians to own their own home. What they refuse to admit publicly is that they are taxing young Australians even more as they save to afford those homes. This trust tax has now impacted the companies, the organisations, the tradies, the Australian small businesses and the Australian family businesses that build those homes.

HIA's managing director, Jocelyn Martin, in a press release, said the proposal would have consequences far beyond taxation, affecting how many small businesses are structured and operated. She also said:
Around three in five HIA members operate through a family trust.
Do you know what HIA members primarily are? They are builders, the people who build the homes that Australians need to live in, which we currently do not have enough of.

This takes me to what I believe is the agenda of this government, and it's becoming very clear. We've spoken about this over and over. We would like Australians to be able to own their own homes. Those opposite would like your super fund to own your own home and for you to be a perpetual renter of that home. That's what they want. That's what the agenda is. Guess what? Your super fund can invest in property, but you can't via your own super or via your SMSF any more, because this government has said that you can't. This is just another layer in that same agenda to make homeownership less accessible for the everyday Australian. It is totally lacking any foresight to think that taxing Australian tradies and taxing Australian builders even more will actually make housing more accessible for people in this country. (Time expired)

Senator ANANDA-RAJAH (Victoria) (15:28): On the topic of trusts, over the last 20 years, we have seen an explosion in discretionary trusts. We now have over 800,000 of them, and they are heavily used by wealthy households. As the former member for Higgins, I represented one of the wealthiest electorates in this country. Trusts were widely used by my constituents. It was driven largely by the top marginal tax rate, which, as you know, is 45 per cent. With the Medicare levy, which is two per cent, it is 47 per cent. People on those incomes are paying a lot of money to the tax man. I'm speaking about the constituents I used to represent. That top 10 per cent shoulder a high tax burden. They account for nearly half of the tax take—around 46 to 50 per cent. So they pay a lot of tax, which pays for all the services and the infrastructure and the things Australians need. They also work really hard.

It's not surprising that, over that time, this top marginal tax rate, which Paul Keating himself described as punitive, has driven a whole series of perverse behaviour, including the use of discretionary trusts as tax shelters—entirely legitimate over this period of time, entirely legal and lawful. The problem now is that we're seeing such leakage of tax and such rising demands on our economy from aged care, from disability, from paying interest on debt, from defence and national security and from climate change—let's not forget climate change. All of these kinds of pressures are intensifying on us, and there is a need for government to raise revenue and to deal with tax leakage, which is something we are boldly trying to do, knowing full well that it's unpopular. But we are a responsible government and we have to deal with these kinds of issues.

What is of concern, however, is the impacts on small businesses. There are 2.7 million small businesses in Australia. They are the backbone of our economy. We think around 210,000 small businesses will be affected by this change. The government has made some concessions to try and help small businesses restructure without incurring high costs, which COSBOA have said could be in the order of $50,000. We also accept that small businesses use these sorts of trusts for asset protection, for succession planning, for continuity, all of which are entirely important and legitimate, and we are consulting deeply with them right now, particularly with industry, with small business as represented by COSBOA and, of course, farmers.

This change in taxation arrangements for discretionary trusts tax is something that we need to be very careful of in this current economic environment. Small businesses are doing it tough. There is weak demand. Costs are high and, unfortunately, at the moment, rising. We've done our level best to help small business with the $20,000 instant asset write-off and the loss carry-back, which they also advocated for and which I'm pleased we could deliver. We are listening and consulting.

Senator GATENBY (Tasmania—Deputy Opposition Whip in the Senate) (15:33): I rise to take note of Minister Wong's answers to questions from Senators Blyth, Colbeck and Ruston on tax on trusts. The Albanese Labor government has once again shown how little it really understands about small businesses and the pressures that they're facing. I, like a multitude of many small-business owners out there at the moment, have seen the tin ear that the Labor Party and the Labor government have shown towards small businesses in recent times. Let's take trusts for the moment. Labor's approach to discretionary trust taxation is causing serious concerns across small businesses, farmers, tradies and many others. Even Labor state governments are now scrambling to protect small businesses from Jim Chalmers latest tax grab. That tells you just how badly this has been handled to date.

Small businesses, including franchises and even small builders, are being given three bad choices: pay more tax, pay accountants and lawyers to restructure or give up the flexibility they've relied on for generations. The NFF says there are more than 37,000 trusts operating in agriculture, fisheries and forestry, but it's still not clear what sorts of farming activities are covered under primary production income. They're asking for certainty, sensible rules and a government that understands the realities of running a business. I know those opposite don't understand this, but for a small-business owner cashflow is everything. It determines whether suppliers are paid, whether rent is met and whether another employee can be hired. I've worked in small business, including our own former family business, and I know the pressures they face. Unlike this government, small-business owners cannot simply spend more money when the numbers don't add up. Yet Labor keeps adding costs, uncertainty and frustration.

Take the recent changes to card surcharges. Banning a surcharge doesn't just eliminate the cost of accepting a card. Just fancy the facepalm when the Prime Minister claimed that the changes would make everyday purchases like your coffee cheaper. One female owner of a Tasmanian hospitality business has told me this week that across two venues her business has now absorbed just under $3,000 in 10 days, including some new fees. This is up from $129 in the corresponding period last year. It forecasts an annual impact of over $120,000, factoring in seasonality—a $120,000 impact!—unless it passes those costs on by increasing prices. Yet Labor thinks the surcharge has simply vanished. It hasn't. Someone pays.

In my short time here, I've heard of so many small businesses saying the same thing under the weight of this government's reforms. If Minister Wong is not hearing those concerns in her office, she should ask herself why. We're listening; the question is whether this government is also listening.

Then came the ATO's plan to stop accepting direct credit card payments for tax. For businesses waiting on overdue invoices, a credit card can provide vital short-term cashflow flexibility. The government was left scrambling on its position. Then there was the hypocrisy. While small businesses were essentially being told to absorb their card processing costs, the ATO wanted to walk away from its own. Small businesses deserve respect, not another round of Labor's moving goalposts and tax grabs on trusts. They don't deserve your higher taxes and energy bills. Labor should back, not break, small businesses.
Question agreed to.

Senator ALLMAN-PAYNE (Queensland) (15:37): I move:
That the Senate take note of the answer given by the Minister representing the Minister for Social Services (Senator Gallagher) to a question without notice I asked today.

I note with some dismay that this government seems utterly ignorant of its role in creating and perpetuating poverty in Australia. You would think that during Anti-Poverty Week, when advocates and people living in poverty are here in Canberra, lobbying the government to do more than just mouth platitudes about doing what they can, Labor would have something significant to offer people who are struggling for survival. Instead, we got the social services minister announcing meagre funding for emergency relief charities amounting to a dollar per welfare recipient—one dollar.

Poverty isn't an accident. It isn't some surprising by-product of policy. It's the result of deliberate choices made by successive governments over decades, and Labor has made the deliberate choice to keep all social security payments below the poverty line. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's latest report on mortality outcomes showed that people accessing the JobSeeker payment are up to 10 times more likely to die than people not on any income support payment. Almost three in five people aged 22 to 64 who passed away over 2012 to 2022 were accessing income support.

More and more Australians are hungry, homeless and desperate, and they are running out of places to turn. We see this every day in my electorate office in Gladstone. Every week, we hear from dozens of constituents who contact us looking for help: help getting into public housing, help navigating Centrelink, help with emergency hampers because they're escaping domestic violence and they haven't eaten in days. With every month that goes by, we hear from more and more people.

The minister, in her answer, said that Labor is the party of job creation. That's all well and good, but unemployment is literally baked into our economy. Unemployment is a tool used by the Reserve Bank to control inflation. We know this. Just last month, RBA governor Michele Bullock said an unemployment rate of 4.5 to five per cent would take the heat out of inflation. What does Labor have to say to the people who, through no fault of their own, are forced into unemployment so that the RBA can make a number on a computer screen go down? Not very much, it seems.

Meanwhile, life is pretty sweet for the gas companies and the billionaires who get richer and richer off the back of Australian workers and Australia's resources. Prosper Australia Research Institute released a report just this week showing that Australia could rake in $45 billion more each year if we properly valued and taxed our resources. We know that if the government simply chose to tax gas exports at 25 per cent, a measure that has massive national support, we could raise $17 billion a year to go towards public housing, affordable groceries and raising the rate of welfare payments.

The social security system is supposed to help people, but it's increasingly complex, highly conditional and riddled with contradictions and inconsistencies. Poverty payments, dodgy debt recovery, punitive compulsory activities, income control regimes—the social security system under Labor resembles Squid Game more than it does a safety net. Choosing to keep people in poverty when you have the tools at your disposal to lift them out of it is indefensible. But it's a choice that this government, a Labor government, continues to make time and time again. I note that the minister said that they have raised income support. Well, it's currently a meagre $400-or-so a week, and I challenge the minister to find a single rental property in this country that someone on income support can afford, let alone put food on the table, pay their bills and keep themself healthy and well.
Question agreed to.

Senator BELL (New South Wales—One Nation Whip) (15:42): I move:
That the Senate take note of the answer given by the Minister representing the Minister for Communications (Senator Farrell) to a question without notice I asked today relating to cybersafety.

I will give this to Senator Farrell. He gave a very succinct answer to my question, which is quite interesting, frankly, because Senator Farrell often gives very long and detailed answers. While his answer to my question was succinct, I would have preferred a more useful one. But you cannot have everything. I asked why Labor won't put its assurances about free speech into the digital duty of care legislation it has put before this parliament. The minister had the chance today to commit to that answer. He had the chance to explain why Labor would not put stronger protections in the legislation. He did not. Apparently, we are supposed to be satisfied because Minister Wells says that there's nothing to worry about. Well, we're passing a law; we're not asking for a character reference here, and there are reasons to be concerned. Experts are concerned.

A gentleman named Michael Shellenberger has been in Australia warning Australians about governments giving themselves more power over what people can and can't say online—governments giving themselves the power to monitor you and restrict your speech. You don't have to agree with everything he's saying to ask why those in power want their power to be so broad. If the government says that we've misunderstood it, it has a fairly straightforward remedy for that: tighten up the wording. Instead, we get this business about mystery shoppers. That is how the government described these sock puppet accounts; it called them 'mystery shoppers'. Labor wants to give government officials fake identities online. It tries to wave that away, saying they are mystery shoppers. But then it can't explain why we need them and, more importantly, why it won't accept clear limits on their use.

Frankly, I don't understand why Labor won't expressly rule out using those accounts on lawful political discussion explicitly in the legislation. It's all well and good to say it, but I would like—and I think many Australians would like—to see it carved in stone in the bill. People are entitled to go online and have their say, have their criticisms of us, all of us. They're entitled to say the Prime Minister is doing a rotten job. They're entitled to argue about immigration or energy policy without wondering whether someone in a government office is acting like a mystery shopper or using a sock puppet account and taking notes or whether a government agency is putting material into that debate as well, because that is in the legislation too. The government can create material and put it online. Australians ought to know if the things that they are reading are coming from the government. They ought to know where it's coming from. Put the department's name on it. There's no need to invent a bloke named Barry who happens to agree with ministers.

I'd ask Labor senators to think more seriously about this. Would you be happy if we had those powers or if the Greens had those powers? I suspect you would want to read the fine print very closely. They certainly wouldn't settle for: 'Don't worry. It'll be alright.' I think they'd be treating it a lot more seriously. I wouldn't expect you to take my word for it, because it works both ways. The law has to protect people regardless of who wins the next election. That means clear restrictions and independent scrutiny, not an annual summary after the event. That is what is in the legislation. They say that the actual information that they have agreed to provide occurs as a sort of annual summary. There's no detailed itemised audit of the information these 'mystery shoppers', as they call them, will be collecting.

No-one is asking Labor to abandon the protection of children or the prosecution of criminals. What we're asking is just to take greater steps to protect lawful speech as well—more scrutiny, more clarity in the legislation. Don't try and wave things away and dismiss them. 'Mystery shoppers' and 'sock puppets' are really silly sounding terms, but they're really serious issues that should be treated seriously by this government. If it is already the government's intention not to do those things, then there should be no argument. Put it in the bill.
Question agreed to.

Senator McALLISTER (New South Wales—Minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme) (15:58): I present the government response to the report of the Senate Economics Legislation Committee on its inquiry into provisions of the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Legislation Amendment (Safety and Other Measures) Bill 2024. Australian Government response to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee report:

span.span: Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Legislation Amendment (Safety and Other Measures) Bill 2024 [Provisions]

p.span: July 2026
The Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Legislation Amendment (Safety and Other Measures) Bill 2024 (Bill) was introduced into the House of Representatives on 15 February 2024.
On 29 February 2024, the Senate referred the provisions of the Bill to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Committee) for inquiry and report by 22 March 2024.
The committee recommended that the Bill be passed.

The Bill passed the Senate on 16 May 2024 with Government amendments that removed Part 2 of Schedule 2 of the Bill and clarified that contractors are included in the protection against discrimination provisions. The Bill passed the House of Representatives on 28 May 2024.

The Bill received Royal Assent on 11 June 2024 and became the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Legislation Amendment (Safety and Other Measures) Act 2024. The last provisions of the Act commenced on 12 June 2025.

In the report, the Committee recommended that the Bill be passed. The three additional dissenting reports from the Australian Greens, Senator David Pocock and Senator Lidia Thorpe each recommended that Part 2 of Schedule 2 of the Bill be removed or the Bill be opposed. Recommendations that the Bill be passed/not passed are not addressed in this Government response.

There are two additional recommendations from the Australian Greens and ten additional recommendations from Senator Lidia Thorpe. The Government's response to each dissenting recommendation is provided below.
Australian Greens' dissenting report—March 2024
Recommendation 2: That the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage legislative framework be amended to ensure that:
First Nations people, Traditional Owners and Knowledge Holders are included in the definition of 'relevant people';
First Nations people, Traditional Owners and Knowledge Holders have a veto power over any developments in their sea country; and

During any consultations for Offshore Project Proposals and/or Environment Plans, proponents are required to identify areas of underwater cultural heritage, both tangible and intangible, how the activity may impact it and how these potential impacts can be avoided or mitigated.
The Government notes this recommendation.

In the 2023-24 Budget, the Government committed $12 million over three years to a review of the environmental management regime for offshore petroleum and greenhouse gas activities to ensure it is fit for purpose for a decarbonising economy. The review will also consider opportunities to provide regulatory and administrative certainty for carbon capture and storage activities.

Consultation with affected stakeholders and communities is an important aspect of Australia's offshore regulatory regime for petroleum and greenhouse gas storage activities. The Offshore Environment Management Review includes a focus on clarifying existing consultation requirements for offshore activities, including with First Nations people and communities, to ensure consultation is targeted and effective.

The Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is considering an approach to First Nations engagement in the context of reforms to Commonwealth environmental and cultural heritage protection laws that is inclusive and respectful of cultural authority.

The Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) (NTA) provides procedural requirements for 'future acts' which have the potential to impact native title rights and interests, including in offshore places (per s 24NA(8) of the NTA). While this does not provide a power of veto to native title holders or claimants, it provides procedural rights at a minimum. The Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) completed its review of the NTA's future acts regime and provided its Final Report to the Attorney-General in March 2026. The report was tabled in Parliament on 24 June 2026.

Recommendation 3: That the Government amend the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) to ensure that the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples is considered within The Statement of Compatibility with Human Rights included in the Explanatory Memorandum, including the principle of free, prior and informed consent, and that the sponsors of bills are required to provide the relevant information to prove that our obligations are being met.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.

The reports of the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights Inquiry into Australia's Human Rights Framework and the Joint Standing Committee on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Inquiry into the application of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in Australia have both made recommendations that the Government amend the definition of 'human rights' in the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 to include the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). The Government is carefully considering these reports.
Senator Lidia Thorpe's dissenting report—March 2024
Recommendation 2: Implement the UNDRIP into domestic law to have full domestic effect and enshrine in law First Peoples' rights to Free, Prior and Informed Consent.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
Refer to the Government's response to the Australian Greens' recommendation 2.
Recommendation 3: Implement all recommendations from the 2023 Inquiry into the application of UNDRIP in Australia.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
Refer to the Government's response to the Australian Greens' recommendation 2.

Recommendation 4: Amend the Parliamentary Scrutiny (Human Rights) Act 2011 to include consideration of UNDRIP, so that no legislation is passed before proper consideration of its engagement and compatibility with the rights of First Peoples.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
Refer to the Government's response to the Australian Greens' recommendation 3.

Recommendation 5: The Albanese Government must fulfil its election commitments to reform national environmental laws, including a National Standard for First Peoples Engagement and Participation in Decision-Making, in this term of government.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
Recommendation 6: The federal government must commence Treaty negotiations with First Peoples as a matter of urgency.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
Recommendation 7: Australia cannot pursue any more new coal and gas projects if we are to meet our emissions reduction obligations under the Paris Agreement.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.

Australia has national emissions reduction targets of 43% by 2030 on 2005 levels, 62-70% by 2035, and Net Zero by 2050. These targets apply to all parts of the economy, and all greenhouse gases. Australia's Net Zero Plan articulates how Australia will transition to a net zero economy, consistent with our international and domestic commitments. The Net Zero Plan is underpinned by six sectoral plans covering all major sectors of the economy, including the resources sector. The resources sector plan will identify opportunities to reduce emissions from all activities in scope, including coal and gas projects.

The Safeguard Mechanism plays a key role in incentivising long-term investment in emissions reduction for the country's largest industrial facilities, including coal mines and gas projects. All covered facilities are required to steadily reduce their emissions through declining emissions limits, or baselines, on a trajectory consistent with achieving Australia's emission reduction targets of 43% below 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero by 2050. Any new facilities have their baselines determined using emissions intensity values set using international best practice levels, recognising the opportunity to build world's best practice emissions performance into their design.

The Government's Future Gas Strategy, echoed in the Net Zero Plan and Resources Sector Plan, establishes that the role of gas will change as we move towards net zero in Australia by 2050. Australian gas will play an important role in an orderly global and domestic energy transformation. Even in net zero scenarios, Australia and the world will need gas through to 2050 and beyond.

Our trading partners have indicated Australia will play a vital role in supplying the resources needed to ensure their energy and economic security as they follow their own path to meet their net zero commitments. The international demand for low emissions fuels and materials underpins our Future Made in Australia ambitions. The Government is investing in the establishment of new industries such as critical minerals processing and low carbon liquid fuels to lower our emissions, attract investment and grow the economy.
Recommendation 8: State and federal governments must grant greater protections and declare critical habitats for cetaceans, including Koontapool/Southern Right Whale.
The Government notes the recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.

The Southern Right Whale is listed as endangered and migratory under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. In September 2023, the Government publicly released updated Biologically Important Areas for the Southern Right Whale. This includes areas used by the species that are important for migration and areas designated as critical for reproduction. The National Recovery Plan for the Southern Right Whale was finalised in 2024 in consultation with state agencies and species experts and includes current scientific information on the species, habitat, identified threats and a range of conservation and management actions required to mitigate potential impacts to the species.
Recommendation 9: Governments must ban seismic blasting and refuse any further fossil fuel projects impacting Sea Country.
The Government does not support this recommendation.

On 9 December 2025, the Government published the revised Offshore Exploration Work Bid Guidelines which included a requirement to apply a technology-neutral approach to seismic acquisition and to minimise seismic surveying, where possible, to align with the Government's Future Gas Strategy.

The Government is committed to protecting our marine environment and enforcing safe and environmentally responsible practices by the offshore resources sector. Offshore exploration and development activities, including seismic surveying, are subject to a robust environmental approvals regime, regulated by the National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority (NOPSEMA). NOPSEMA employs qualified technical experts with experience in offshore environmental impact and risk management, marine ecology and environmental science.

Environment plans for proposed seismic surveys must demonstrate that any impacts and risks associated with the activity have been evaluated, and that controls have been adopted to reduce those impacts and risks to as low as reasonably practicable and to acceptable levels. If the environmental impacts of a proposed seismic survey cannot be managed, NOPSEMA will not allow the activity to proceed.

The Government's Future Gas Strategy outlines a pathway for Australia to manage its evolving role as a trusted gas producer and as a responsible climate actor which acts with transparency, integrity, and from a strong evidence base. As the Future Gas Strategy states, gas will continue to play an important role in Australia's transition to net zero.

The Government recognises the importance of First Nations people's connection to country and is committed to improving social and economic outcomes through future energy projects. Offshore titleholders must consult with relevant persons under the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage (Environment) Regulations 2023, which may include Traditional Owners and other cultural knowledge holders, during the preparation of an environment plan, and demonstrate how impacts and risks will be mitigated.
Recommendation 10: The government must implement in full all recommendations from the 2021 A Way Forward Report into the destruction of Juukan Gorge.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
The Government is continuing to implement the recommendations agreed under A Way Forward, as outlined in the 2022 Government response to the destruction of Juukan Gorge.
Recommendation 11: Political donations from fossil fuel companies and other harmful industries should be banned.
The Government notes this recommendation.
This recommendation is not within the scope of the Bill.
The Government has clear commitments to improve transparency and accountability across our electoral system.
Following the 2022 election, the Government asked the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters (JSCEM) to inquire into and report on various matters, including political donations.
JSCEM did not recommend banning donations from specific donors. It did, however, recommend the Government consider ways to provide greater transparency of political donations.

In February 2025, the Government's historic reforms to the electoral system to improve public transparency and impose limits on political donations were passed by the Parliament. These new laws will come into effect 1 January 2027.

The Government believes electoral reform should be undertaken in a consultative and multipartisan manner and looks forward to continued engagement with colleagues across the Parliament on electoral reforms.

Senator O'NEILL (New South Wales) (16:02): I rise to take note of the government response to the report on financial abuse undertaken by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services. It's a title that has a little tag at the end that says it's an 'insidious form of domestic violence'. There are a few people here in the chamber, but there are also people who might be listening online. I want to give you confidence that the democratic project, as much as it's maligned in the public place, is actually working.

The impact of financial abuse being perpetrated on people in Australia is worth $5.7 billion. It does happen to some men, but predominantly this is an issue that affects women. We all know about scams. We know how bad they are. We know how they hurt people that we love. They take money away from people who need it—illegally. That costs $3 billion. Think about that. Nearly twice as much damage to the Australian population from financial abuse is often done by somebody's partner.

Great Australians—and champions, advocates and lobbyists for those Australians—came into this place and told their stories. We went to Perth, and we heard stories about a woman who was coerced into taking on debt for her partner to buy a car that she didn't want to buy. He coerced her physically and emotionally into doing that and then, not too long after, beat her to such a pulp that she suffered a permanent brain injury. She spent time in a coma, for six months, and woke up with a debt that had escalated and escalated—and she could not get any relief from the provider of that financial instrument.

This is the scale of what's going on. The government has been listening to much of this evidence and other evidence about the problem with financial products and also with the weaponising of the instruments of government, such as the ATO. In this government, we are really committed to support. This was a unanimous report. I know the headlines are all about people who hate one another here, but, every now and then, we really get it together—Labor, Greens and the Liberal-National coalition. There were 61 recommendations, with 58 of them accepted. We are committed to preventing perpetrators of family abuse from receiving victim's superannuation and death benefits. How wrong is it that that has been able to occur? We're fixing that. Coerced directorships are where people's names and signatures are just copied by their partners for 10, 12, 20 different companies, and they don't even realise that they're acquiring debt in their own name because their partners are so deceptive. We can't allow these things to continue. You won't see the director identification number in a headline; there won't be a whole lot of noise and fireworks about that, but this is real government with really good senators and members working properly in our democracy to give the things that we need to function properly as a harmonious society to the Australian people—where we pick out issues and go: 'That is not okay, that is not fair, and that is not the Australian way. We are going to do something about it, and we're legislating for change.'

The ATO is often the instrument that sees where these debts have been accrued, and many, many women talked abut the ATO arriving at their door and saying, 'Well, look, you've got all this debt'—hundreds of thousands of dollars, sometimes millions of dollars!—'the only way you can get out of it, love, is by signing this form, and you will become a bankrupt.' Women who didn't even know they were directors have been saddled with this incredible debt. The malice of some of the people who are perpetrating this in our economy and in our society is truly shocking. We had evidence from one woman whose husband pulled apart the family finances, loaded it up with as much debt as possible on his way out the door, sold his house—sold their house—to his mate at a reduced price and made sure that his wife and their three children were out of that house two weeks before the daughter turned 18 because he didn't want them to have a party there.

There are awful people who need the law to be a barrier to prevent them from doing what they are doing. This committee has documented this shameful practice. It's no longer in the dark; we brought it out into the light. This government now has five ministers involved in advancing change to improve the outcomes—$5.7 billion ripped off by one Australian against their intimate partners and their own children. Then, the whole of the public purse has to try and help hold that together. We are talking about women who are suffering debt for decades after they leave a terrible situation. I encourage you: be confident that our democracy is working, read the report, and watch this government get it done. I seek leave to continue my remarks later.
Leave granted; debate adjourned.
Northern Australia Joint Committee
Report
Senator DEAN SMITH (Western Australia) (16:07): I move:
That the Senate take note of the report.

I rise to speak on the tabling of this important report by the Joint Standing Committee on Northern Australia. At its heart is a simple question: if northern Australia is so important to our prosperity, energy security and national defence, why do we continue to govern it as if it were simply an extension of southern Australia? For decades, governments have produced plans and programs for the north, yet the same barriers remain: distance, high costs, inadequate infrastructure, workforce shortages, fragmented approvals and governments operating in silos. This report argues that it's a time for a reset. Nowhere is that more apparent than in Western Australia's far north-west. The Pilbara is one of Australia's great economic engine rooms. Its iron ore, gas and resources industries generate enormous export wealth and underpin national prosperity. Further north, the Kimberley holds enormous untapped potential in resources, agriculture, energy and tourism.

But we will never realise that potential if we treat the north simply as somewhere people fly in, extract wealth and fly out again. Northern development must mean building permanent communities—places where people can live, raise families and build businesses. That requires roads, ports and airports as well as housing, reliable energy, water, telecommunications, schools and health services. We also need to confront one of the great weaknesses in the way the government has approached the north. One-size-fits-all regulation is not the answer. Too much regulation is designed around the circumstances of Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra and then applied uniformly across the continent. Why should a regulatory model designed for a large metropolitan market or population centre automatically be right for Kununurra, Derby or the Pilbara? The distances are greater, markets are thinner, workforces are smaller, infrastructure is limited and costs are higher. A regulation that is a minor impost in Melbourne could kill an investment in the Kimberley. Uniformity is not fairness. National standards do not require identical regulation everywhere. That is why it's time again to think seriously about designated accelerated development areas across northern Australia. We should identify places of national economic and strategic importance and deliberately create the conditions for investment, development and permanent population growth. A designated development accelerated area could bring together regulatory relief, accelerated coordinated approvals, infrastructure planning and targeted incentives. Instead of proponents navigating multiple agencies, governments and approval processes, give them a coordinated pathway with clear requirements and firm timeframes. This is not a regulatory free-for-all. Standard should remain high, environmental protection should remain robust, and native title and cultural heritage obligations must be respected. But the process can be faster, clearer and better coordinated.

Tax policy must also be at the heart of this discussion. The zone tax offset has not been indexed for more than two decades. The fringe benefits tax can penalise employers for providing the housing, transport and assistance needed to attract and retain workers in remote communities. Capital gains tax settings can discourage investment in exploration and emerging industries. We cannot say we want people in investment in northern Australia while maintaining settings that make that harder, nor can infrastructure remain an afterthought. We should identify now the roads, ports, power, water and communications needed to unlock the next generation of development across the Pilbara and the Kimberley. Infrastructure should not simply follow development. Done properly, it creates development. The Pilbara has already shown what northern Western Australia can deliver for the whole nation. The Kimberley shows how much more remains possible.

Our ambition should be a stronger, more populated and more productive north-west, supporting new industries, strengthening our sovereign capability and carrying a greater share of Australia's future prosperity. Accelerated development zones should be part of this ambition. Build the infrastructure, tailor regulation to northern conditions, get the tax settings right, give investors certainty and give more Australians a reason to make the north their permanent home. Developing the Pilbara and unlocking the Kimberley is not regional assistance; it's nation building. We know the opportunity. This report provides some direction. Now, we need the determination to deliver on this ambition.
Question agreed to.

Artificial Intelligence
Senator LAMBIE (Tasmania) (16:13): I move:
That the Senate—

a. acknowledges the growing threat posed by artificial intelligence (AI), deepfakes, voice cloning and other emerging technologies, which are increasingly being exploited to impersonate individuals and organisations, spread disinformation, manipulate the public and facilitate sophisticated scams and fraud;
b. expresses serious concern regarding the lack of protection from AI-generated political advertising which undermines electoral integrity, democratic accountability and public trust; and

c. calls on the Government to urgently strengthen Australia's legislative and regulatory framework to address the misuse of AI, deepfakes and voice cloning and prevent their malicious use in scams, fraud and impersonation, including in political advertising.

Before the last election, the ABC asked me to take part in an AI experiment. They asked if I could clone my voice using cheap AI tools. They wanted to see if people in Burnie, in my own backyard, would know my voice from an 'AI fake Jacqui', as they called it. Well, that was scary enough. But here we are two years later, and the deepfake technology is even scarier. A deepfake video of Angus Taylor and me having an argument on ABC TV's Insiders show has been doing the rounds on social media for months. My office has done all the right things. We got straight out on the socials, warning people, but it's still popping up. Just for the record, Australians, I don't endorse any companies, especially not insurance companies. I work for the people of Tasmania, full stop—no endorsing.

In the last sitting, an AI deepfake video of me popped up, and it's doing the rounds again. It's an even nastier one. It's a video of a fake AI Jacqui telling One Nation supporters they are vile and disgusting. And who is sharing this nasty AI slop? Well, you wouldn't guess. After our investigation—a One Nation supporter, of course. We have also alerted the AFP. This is the sort of vile political advertising that just causes more division. I would like to ask every One Nation senator in this place if you support this sort of rubbish. Is this what you call free speech, is it? When we reported it to Facebook Meta, you wouldn't guess what they said. They told us that this video didn't breach their community standards. You know why they said that? Because, let's face it, when it comes to Meta and Facebook, they have no standards, full stop.

I'm looking forward to seeing the government's duty of care bill. This kind of fake, hideous content causes hatred and division, so I get why One Nation likes it; hatred and division are all they've got up their sleeve. As I've said before, I don't care about me, but I do care about my staff who have to deal with the One Nation troll army almost every day—every day! And I care about Australians who are seeing this and might think that it's real.

Australia has strong laws to protect consumers from false claims made in advertisements. Pharmaceutical companies can't claim to have a cure for cancer, food companies can't claim that sugary foods are good for our children, and lawyers cannot guarantee they will win every personal injury case. But it's still okay in this country and legal to lie in political ads. But we can change that. South Australia has had truth-in-political-advertising laws since the 1980s. In 2020, the ACT Legislative Assembly unanimously passed truth-in-political-advertising laws that came into effect in July 2021. Parties and candidates in Australia get a lot of taxpayer money with very few strings attached. What if some of that money gets turned into political ads that are misleading or deceptive? Truth-in-political-advertising laws are extremely popular. There's been a lot of polling on this, and nine out of 10 Australians want truth-in-political-advertising rules, full stop.

Professor Terry Flew is the coordinator of the centre for artificial intelligence at Sydney university. The professor told the Joint Select Committee on AI that his one immediate recommendation is 'that the current political advertising laws be changed to prohibit the use of AI generated deepfakes in election campaigns'—in other words, truth-in-political-advertising laws. Professor Flew told the committee that political deepfakes go way beyond 'the legitimate bounds of public campaigning and prove to be genuinely threatening to the individuals and groups who are the targets of them'.

AI is completely out of control. We know that because the big tech bros are the ones warning the world that there needs to be more regulation and guardrails. It's coming from them. Now, it would appear that our government has finally woken up—well, maybe. I'm hoping. In February this year, when I asked the minister why we weren't investing in our own Australian made AI, all the minister could say was that Australia was a great place to invest, and he pointed to the AI Safety Institute, which has no actual powers, Australians—just another little bunch of people up there getting paid some cash. By the way, this was just days after Labor got rid of the independent AI advisory group. Go figure. So the only place they were getting their information from was big tech.

Last weekend's TheSaturday Paper had a very interesting story about the number of top-level staffers with close ties to the Labor Party who have left the Labor Party and are now working with big tech. The article spoke to insiders who pointed to big tech using the same tactics as big tobacco. Aren't you disgusting little people? That involves hiring multiple former Labor staff. And Ed Husic, the former industry minister who led the government's initial response to AI, said:
What we're witnessing is nothing more than a shock and awe lobbying approach by US tech, designed to swamp government decision-making.
An AI strategist who has worked inside and outside government made a similar point:

The amount of power these people have is incomprehensible … This isn't just a product that's being sold. This is dual-use capability. This is the equivalent of a private company developing nuclear weapons.

This government and the last Liberal government let social media get out of control. Well, you're on notice now. Australia is watching. We need controls on AI now, and we need to ban political deepfake ads. There is already a huge problem with trust in our politicians and this place up here. Having strong truth in political advertising laws and banning political deepfakes would go a long way to having a very good start. I have to ask: what are you waiting for? What I see as the form of policing out there is that you're actually putting the lives of all these parliamentarians and their staff in danger. You are doing that.

Until you bring in some rules and regulations, this is going to continue to uplift. You are setting a very dangerous precedent for one of us to be hurt. God help us if someone goes at me and one of my staff gets hurt. It's gone too far! You have to do something about this, for God's sake, for at least the safety and welfare of our own staff in our offices who travel with us all the time. We are not the PM. We don't have security around us. It is getting that vicious out there. It might be okay for a backbencher who is not known out there, and that is no disrespect to you. But, for an Independent like myself who's been up here for over 10 years and whose face is out there everywhere, and everyone knows who I am, I am extremely worried about my staff being around me. That is a problem. I am really worried. So, please, before one of us or one of our staff actually gets hurt, before it is too late, I'm begging you to do something about this.
Question agreed to.

Glenorchy Medicare Mental Health Centre

Senator CAROL BROWN (Tasmania) (16:23): Tonight I rise to recognise the important new service for the people of Glenorchy and surrounding communities, the Glenorchy Medicare Mental Health Centre. Earlier this month, I was proud to join the Assistant Minister for Mental Health and Suicide Prevention, Emma McBride; the Assistant Minister for Health and Aged Care and member for Lyons, Rebecca White; and centre staff and members of the local community to officially open this new service in the heart of Glenorchy.

The centre is located in the former Snows Dry Cleaning building, a familiar local landmark designed by the renowned Tasmanian architect Esmond Dorney in the late 1950s. Esmond's son, architect Paddy Dorney, was present and spoke at the opening, reflecting on the building's enduring place in the hearts of local people and its renewal for a new chapter of community service. It is fitting that a building with such a strong place in Glenorchy's history has been thoughtfully renewed to serve the community for many years to come. Its architectural character has been preserved by creating a warm, safe and welcoming environment.

The Glenorchy Medicare Mental Health Centre provides free and confidential mental health care with no appointment or referral required. It's open Monday to Friday. People can simply walk through the door and speak with qualified mental health professionals and peer workers with lived experience. They can receive immediate assistance, short- and medium-term support and help connecting with other health, housing, employment and social services. The centre also offers information and advice to carers, families and friends. That simple walk-in model matters.

Reaching out for help can be difficult, and the mental health system can be hard to navigate, particularly when someone is already in distress. Cost, waiting times, referrals and uncertainty about where to go can all be barriers. This centre removes many of those barriers. It gives people a clear local front door and the reassurance that support is available close to home when they need it. We know that one in five adults experience mental health challenges each year. Behind that statistic are individuals, family, friends and colleagues. Nobody should feel they have to struggle alone, and no-one should miss out on care because they cannot afford it or do not have a referral.

The Glenorchy centre is fully funded by the Australian government, commissioned by Primary Health Tasmania and operated by Stride mental health. Its multidisciplinary team includes mental health clinicians, counsellors, social workers and peer workers. The contribution of peer workers is especially important. Lived experience brings understanding, trust and human connection to care. As one of the peer workers said at the opening, recovery does not always happen in a straight line. Sometimes the most important thing we can offer is to listen without judgement, treat people with respect and remind them that there can always be a way forward.

The Glenorchy Centre is the 57th Medicare mental health centre to open nationally. In Tasmania, it joins existing services in Launceston, Devonport and Burnie which have already delivered more than 22,000 free walk-in appointments across Tasmania. Nationally, the network has provided more than half a million free walk-in appointments. These numbers demonstrate both the demand for accessible mental health care and the difference these centres are already making. The Albanese Labor government is investing $1.1 billion in mental health and wellbeing to strengthen services, grow the workforce and deliver care wherever Australians live. The national network of Medicare mental health centres will expand to 92 by mid-2030, including a new full centre at Brighton. This is a practical investment in universal community care.

I thank everyone who has helped bring this centre to life. I acknowledge Primary Health Tasmania, Stride mental health, the centre's clinical and non-clinical staff, peer workers, community organisations, Glenorchy City Council and the local health and support services and their work in helping to build a coordinated local network so that people can find the right support at the right time.

This centre represents the best of Medicare: free, high-quality care available to everyone. I'm proud of our government and particularly Assistant Minister Emma McBride for making mental healthcare easier to access closer to home and free at the point of care. The Glenorchy Medicare Mental Health Centre will make a real difference, and I look forward to seeing it become a trusted and valued part of the community.
