Senator DEAN SMITH (Western Australia) (16:28): I rise this afternoon to recognise the Brabham Gujarati community and the wonderful Garba night recently held in Beechboro. It was a night filled with colour, music, dance, food and, above all, a tremendous sense of community. Garba is one of the great traditions of Gujarati culture, bringing people together through music and dance in celebration of faith, family and community. What was particularly striking was the energy in the room and the number of families and young people taking part in the celebration.

Events such as this play an important role in keeping cultural traditions alive and in passing them from one from one generation to the next. They also give the wider Western Australian community an opportunity to experience and enjoy the extraordinary cultural diversity that has become such an important part of Western Australia. WA's Indian community continues to make an enormous contribution to our economic, professional, cultural and community life.
Senator Ghosh: Hear, hear!

Senator DEAN SMITH: Senator Ghosh is cheering from the sidelines. The Gujarati community is an important part of that story. Community events on this scale do not happen by themselves; they require months of preparation and the commitment of people willing to give their time freely for the benefit of others. I particularly acknowledge and congratulate the organisers and the many volunteers whose hard work made the evening possible. I also congratulate the many thousands of people who came together on that night to celebrate. It was a privilege to share in such a vibrant celebration of Gujarati culture and community in Western Australia. Jai Mata Di.

I'd like to recognise this evening Nepal Festival Perth 2026 and the contribution of the Nepalese community to Western Australia. Since beginning in 2014, the festival has grown into an important celebration of Nepalese culture, bringing thousands of people together to experience Nepal's music, dance, food, heritage and traditions. This year's celebration carries particular significance following the devastating floods across Nepal and the Himalayan region. Lives have been lost, homes and livelihoods have been destroyed and many Western Australian families have faced the anguish of watching events unfold thousands of kilometres away. Yet, from tragedy, we have again seen the strength, generosity and resilience of the Nepalese community. That same spirit was evident at Nepal Festival Perth—people coming together, supporting one another and proudly sharing their heritage with the wider Western Australian community.

Australia and Nepal share more than six decades of diplomatic relations, but the strongest foundation of that friendship has been and will continue to be our people-to-people ties. In Western Australia, the Nepalese community makes an important contribution across business, education, professions and community organisations. The festival represents multiculturalism at its best: Australians proud of where they've come from, proud of the country they now call home and eager to share their traditions with others. I especially congratulate the Non-Resident Nepali Association Western Australia and the organisers, volunteers, performers, sponsors and community organisations who made the festival possible. I extend my warmest and best wishes again to the Nepalese community of Western Australia and to the people of Nepal.

subdebateinfo.title: Raise Our Voice in Parliament, Housing

p.span: Raise Our Voice in Parliament
Housing

Senator BARBARA POCOCK (South Australia) (16:32): I'm honoured to deliver a speech this evening that was written by Kade, a 16-year-old South Australian, as part of the Raise Our Voice in Parliament campaign. It's a delight to welcome Kade and his mum, Brooke, all the way from Port Pirie and from the school St Mark's College. It's a long way to travel to bring your words to this place. Kade says:
A significant issue shaping my future and others, is housing affordability.
Young Australians are being asked to work harder than ever before for opportunities that are further away.
My parent's generation could work and save to realise the great Australian Dream of buying a home, start a family, and build a secure and safe future.

In 2026, young people are not sure if these opportunities will exist. With rising house costs, increasing expenses, and job uncertainties challenging the way my generation is thinking about life and their futures.
This speech isn't about 'getting money'. It's about gaining hope and security for our futures. It's about believing that hard work is going to translate to securing economic stability.

I propose that parliament consider long term decisions that put our futures, and future generations at the centre of policy making. Investing in affordable housing, strengthening education systems, and providing more training and learning opportunities will support young people to believe they have a genuine chance at realising the great Australian Dream.
My generation is left wondering, are we working hard enough?
We are.
My question is, "Will the opportunities that built Australia still be available to future generations?".

Thank you, Kade, for your speech, for your thoughtfulness and for bringing to this Senate today the wishes and thoughts of you and your generation—year 11 at St Mark's College in Port Pirie. They are very important sentiments to bring here. As someone who has recently completed a tour of the whole of our country—talking to young people, to organisations and to academics about what's going on in our housing market—I can tell you that your sentiments are spot-on. We need a long-term plan. We need both major parties—everyone in the Senate and this parliament—to look to the future of our 16-year-olds. Will they be able to afford a home, when their wages now are so much less than the house prices they confront? Will they be able to save a deposit, when the average rent in our country now is over $700 a week?

As we talked about today, there is so little rental accommodation in a place like Port Pirie. House prices across our regional towns, like Port Pirie, are really through the roof. It didn't used to be like this. It used to be that you could find a house in country towns across our nation. I know that, in Lameroo, the little town I grew up in, there were always vacant properties, and you could afford the rent, and you could afford to get into them if you saved your money. That is not possible now across our country.

House prices are up by 400 per cent since 1999, driving a stake into the aspirations and hopes of so many young people like Kade, and causing great worry and concern for people like Brooke, his mum. We want to see our kids into secure housing because secure housing is the foundation for a decent life. It's the basis of finding a job. You need a good home to be able to put yourself through uni and education. You need the stability of rental accommodation if you're going to get a qualification. We know that, if you're going to hold down a job, have a career and start a family, the building block, the foundation for it, is a home. For too many Australians—for the third of Australians who are renters—accumulating a deposit, which used to take around six years on average across our country, now takes 12 years. It's incredibly hard for young people, often with accumulating HECS debts, to look optimistically out from their lives and have a confident hope that they will have a home from which to start their families.

So I say to Kade and his generation: don't stop hoping. Don't stop asking this parliament to respond to your wishes, which are just the same as the wishes that my generation and many generations before had: the chance for a secure household, the chance to accumulate a deposit and get into a home, the chance to be able to afford a mortgage and the chance not to have an overwhelming HECS debt which means running into further debt makes life very, very stressful.
Best of luck with your law degree, Kade. We look forward to seeing you back here in the future.
Education
Employment

Senator GHOSH (Western Australia) (16:37): We begin our lives by participating in a kind of cosmic lottery. None of us chooses where we start life or where we are born. We do not choose our parents or our postcode or the skills or opportunities that are available to us when we are young. As a society, we must recognise that people begin their lives from different starting points, and, as a parliament, we must use that to inform our decision-making. We cannot make all things equal, but, if we make sure that all Australians have the same opportunity to realise their potential and contribute to our society and our economy, we'll be making a good start. The opportunity to access a high-quality education; to hold a secure job with decent pay and conditions; to own a home; to spend time with loved ones, family and friends; and to retire with dignity—we must endeavour to create a nation where opportunity is shared, progress is embraced, hard work is compensated and economic success is abundant and shared.

Education is at the heart of opportunity. Education expands opportunity and reduces inequality in a way that is fundamental and transformative. Education transforms lives. We must invest in early education, properly fund our primary and high schools, empower people to get a trade or a vocational qualification at TAFE and ensure our universities remain the best in the world. We must focus on improving infrastructure in our regional and remote communities across the country when it comes to education and making sure that people who live in our regions have the same educational opportunities as those who live in our cities. It is our responsibility to provide every Australian the chance to be a good student, a good worker and a good employer.
The benefits of education are not just vocational, of course. A good education, whatever form that takes, adds meaning to life and fosters human flourishing.

We must also be committed to secure and well-paid jobs. A commitment to securing a better deal for workers in this country is a core objective of the Australian Labor Party and of the trade union movement. Human labour must never be treated as just a commodity. Workers are not economic inputs. Their lives are not just units to be added up on a balance sheet. Employment provides workers with more than just income; it provides dignity, security, purpose and opportunity. Every worker deserves respect. Every worker deserves to be paid fairly. Every worker deserves to return home safely at the end of the day.

Outside of a person's love and their friendship, the most sacred thing that they can give is their labour. Those who share their labour, who give their labour in that way, deserve to be paid liveable wages and deserve to share in the economic success of our country. As a barrister, I acted on behalf of trade unions and individuals in a range of cases involving underpayment, wrongful termination and the proliferation of sham enterprise agreements. I've seen the lengths people will go to pay workers less and to undermine our industrial relations system, and I am familiar with the cost, the time and the work required to expose and prove that wrongdoing and to rectify those faults.

Individual workers often do not have the power to represent themselves on an equal footing with their employers, and it is the role of trade unions and the industrial relations system to serve as a counterweight to that inherent inequality. We must have strong safety nets in place for workers, and there must be robust mechanisms so workers can negotiate their pay and conditions and are able to stand up for their rights without fear of reprisal from their employers.

I have a great sense of optimism about Australia and the bright future that awaits our wonderful country. I believe in an Australia where people can build a prosperous and happy future for themselves and their families. I believe we can have a strong economy which shares its growth with those who participate in it. I believe in an Australia where fairness is a core national endeavour. And I believe in an Australia where opportunity, progress and fairness are delivered through education; through economic growth; through strong, secure and well-paid jobs; and through productive work. I believe in Australia. I believe in our future and that our best days are ahead of us.

subdebateinfo.title: Raise Our Voice in Parliament, Energy, Goldmining Industry: McPhillamys Gold Project

p.span: Raise Our Voice in Parliament
Energy
Goldmining Industry: McPhillamys Gold Project

Senator LIDDLE (South Australia—Deputy Opposition Whip in the Senate) (16:42): I'm delighted to share these thoughts from Chase, who lives in the electorate of Spence in Adelaide's northern suburbs. I'll now read their submission which was part of the Raise Our Voice in Parliament campaign. Chase has rightly identified the energy decisions you make today will shape the Australia and future generations tomorrow. Chase says:
We need reliable, low-emission electricity for decades to come, yet we continue to prohibit one of our greatest opportunities: nuclear energy.
Australia holds around one-third of the world's economic uranium resources, roughly twice the share of Kazakhstan, which ranks second.
We mine it.
We export it.
Yet we refuse to seriously consider using it ourselves.
Renewables are important, but nuclear offers something different.
Wind turbines typically last 20 to 25 years, while modern nuclear plants can operate for 60 years or more.
Nuclear produces electricity day and night, regardless of weather with a comparative footprint of less land.
Nuclear should also be judged by modern technology, not Chernobyl.
Modern reactors operate under vastly different safety standards.
Nuclear requires investment and responsible waste management, but these are challenges to solve, not reasons for prohibition.

At 16 years old, Chase is asking parliament to remove the nuclear power prohibitions contained in the EPBC Act and the ARPANS Act. Australia's uranium has been mined since 1954. It is the largest known uranium resource in the world, at almost a third of the global total. Australia has the capability. Australia needs the courage to use it. Chase, you have thought deeply about this. Thank you for recognising the importance of an energy mix that includes nuclear to power Australia and reduce emissions.

I'd like to continue on the theme of resources and the energy mix, because we do need energy from sources that make sure that we can keep the lights on and prices low. I'm talking about the energy mix: Chase talked about nuclear; I'm talking about coal; I'm talking about renewables; I'm talking about gas; and wind—it's all in there. It's all necessary to keep our prices low and the lights on.

Earlier today, I heard the Labor Party talk about economic development for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. A little fact that people often forget is that one of the biggest employers of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people is actually the energy sector—bigger than the Commonwealth government. How's that! And they've been doing it for years. People are employed across a range of industries—not just in the industry itself, but also in supplying and providing services to the industry.

We need to make sure we support those industries that support the local communities that live around them. Economic participation and opportunity are critical and they ensure that people can participate in society in the way that they wish to.

We met, this week, here at Parliament House, with the Australian Energy Producers, and hosted a group of people who are benefiting from the industry itself. They were telling us they worked in contracting; they worked in engineering; they worked in aviation; they worked in cultural heritage. They were all committed, and supportive of the jobs that are created by the energy sector. It was really terrific to hear their stories.

This week we also heard about the big fail that was the decision of a Commonwealth minister in the McPhillamys goldmine. A Federal Court judge has found an Aboriginal protection order that halted an approved goldmine was invalid. Who'd have known! A local traditional owner said they didn't know about that bumblebee, but, no, the government went ahead and declared it invalid. Well, that's what the Federal Court just did. But in that time there's been a lost opportunity for jobs and employment. I heard from people who were ramping up the opportunity to take up those businesses, all the time while this project was delayed by the stroke of a pen by a minister who got caught up in ideology rather than common sense.

p.span: Western Australia: Child Care
Raise Our Voice in Parliament

Senator PAYMAN (Western Australia—Australia's Voice Whip) (16:47): It was through Instagram that the then Labor candidate for Durack Karen Wheatland brought glad tidings to her followers in WA's Wheatbelt. Stuffed animal in hand, Ms Wheatland beamed as she announced that a re-elected Labor government would invest $5 million for a new childcare centre in Mukinbudin. Excellent! There's a shortage of quality early childhood education centres in regional WA, and, while the Albanese government doesn't always honour its election commitments, if we've learned anything from the recent grants rorts saga, it's that this government honours its pork-barrelling commitments, right? Could it be that, like Ms Wheatland's Instagram account, this commitment was abandoned immediately after the election?

I tried to use Labor's broken FOI system to see if there was anything more I could learn about the progress on this commitment. The only new document they'd released was a brief to the minister from May. The single line dedicated to Mukinbudin read, 'The department last met with the Shire of Mukinbudin in October 2025.' Then, in a meeting yesterday, the government told the shire that the election promise will not be honoured, due to a lack of demonstrated demand. This is despite the minister describing the commitment, at estimates in February, as 'part of our building early childhood education fund that is building services in underserved areas'. So there's a lack of demand, but they're also 'underserved'. Make it make sense! The Shire of Mukinbudin is being made an example of: 'You didn't elect our candidate, so you're not going to get to build the childcare centre.' I wonder if the PM's Marrickville Golf Club had any issues with getting their taxpayer funded non-competitive grant. This is just another example of this government's east coast bias. When it comes to election promises, they get the pork; we get the barrel.

I want to now finish off the speeches from young West Australians as part of the Raise Our Voice in Parliament campaign. Nineteen-year-old Jamie writes: 'I've always believed in optimism, but this is becoming harder by the day. Despite the scientific consensus and increasingly severe natural disasters, Australia continues to drag its feet on climate change. The cost of inaction won't be measured in dollars but in lives. In an already volatile world, climate change acts as a threat multiplier. Modelling shows that over the next century we'll see tens of millions of premature deaths. We are at the brink of the greatest tragedy in human history. The good news is that we already have the core technologies to address it. We just need the political will. Decarbonisation won't be easy, so it's vital to seize the low-hanging fruit. An essential first step is to halt the approval of new fossil fuel projects. The IPCC, the IEA and the WHO could not have been clearer on this, but Australia hasn't got the memo. I would like parliament to stop sitting on two chairs. It's time to legislate a nationwide ban on new coal and gas extraction projects. Australia has a legacy of baked-in fossil fuels, but now we have a chance to rewrite it. We can prove to the world that this fight can be won.'

Twenty-one-year-old Amelia writes: 'I know my life expectancy is only 79 years old, six years less than the average in Western Australia. I know I'm four times more likely to die in a car crash, three times more likely to die a medically avoidable death, two times more likely to die of heart failure. My future is fundamentally different, all because I grew up in and will return to regional Western Australia. There is a divide between the regions and the cities, and this divide is only growing, swallowing the future of regional Australians. The common solution for this issue is, "Just relocate to the city." It isn't that simple. Regional areas of Australia are the backbone of this country. We should have services which are on par with metropolitan areas. We shouldn't have to decide between living in a place we love or basic services. I ask parliament to consider regional Australia not just as an afterthought. I ask you to invest in our infrastructure, support our education, our health care and our access to essential services. Our lives shouldn't be worth less simply because of where we live. I ask this parliament to invest in regional Australia and change our future.'
I thank Jamie, Amelia and all the other young Western Australians for their dedication and their ideas and for sending those speeches to us, and I wish them all the very best.
